Title/name of problem: Iskovskikh classification of 3-folds
Short description of problem (100 words: This is a famous old result, but a very complicated one and it may be a good idea to revisit it. Riemann surfaces fall into 3 classes - 1)  complex projective line also called Riemann sphere, 2) elliptic curves 3) curves of genus 2 and more, with spherical, flat and hyperbolic geometry respectively. In complex dimension two, the analogue of this is Kodaira's classification of surfaces, and the analogue of Riemann sphere are Del Pezzo surfaces. In dimension 3 and more they are called Fano 3,4,5..folds. Iskovitch classified Fano 3-folds in the seventies.
Reference/source material: https://doi.org/10.1070/IM1977v011n03ABEH001733
Desired outcome: The problem is to learn what Fano means, understand classification in Dimensions 1,2. Check classication in dimension 3, and finally see what prevents these methods from extending to higher dimensions.

Title/name of problem: Robertson-Seymour Graph Minor Theorem
Short description of problem (100 words: This foundational result in modern graph theory proves that any family of graphs which is closed under taking minors can be characterized by a finite set of forbidden minors.
Reference/source material:
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robertson%E2%80%93Seymour_theorem
This article summarizes the state of affairs; that the proof is distributed over a sequence of papers, titled "Graph Minors. N." for N ranging from 1 up 20, published in the 80s, 90s, and 2000s from Robertson and Seymour.

e.g., "Neil Robertson and Paul Seymour, Graph Minors. XX. Wagner's conjecture, Journal of Combinatorial Theory, Series B 92 (2004), 325-357, and the earlier Graph Minors papers it relies on.
https://web.math.princeton.edu/~pds/papers/GM20/GM20.pdf"
Desired outcome:
It would be good to shorten and simplify this long and complicated proof as much as possible.

A Lean proof of the graph minor theorem, including the structural results it depends on. A reusable library for graph minors, tree decompositions, and the finite forbidden-minor characterization would also be valuable.

Title/name of problem: Definability of the Turing jump
Short description of problem (100 words: Slaman and Shore (1999) proved that the Turing jump is definable in the first order theory of the Turing degrees. However, their proof is complicated and does not give a simple definition of the jump. Is there one? Conversely, how far can we go with negative results: prove that there is no Sigma_n definition for n=1,2,3,...?
Reference/source material: Shore and Slaman, Defining the Turing Jump, Math. Res. Lett. 6 (1999), no. 5-6, 711–722
Desired outcome: Use AI to come up with a more explicit definition of the jump in the partial order of the Turing degrees, or prove restrictions on any such definition.

Title/name of problem: Unrepresentable finite lattice
Short description of problem (100 words: OpenAI solved the finite lattice representation problem by finding a finite lattice that is not isomorphic to the congruence lattice of any finite algebra. However, the minimum size of such a lattice is open. It is known that it is at least 8, and OpenAI gave some astronomical upper bounds. Can we narrow it down further?
Reference/source material: https://github.com/openai/math/tree/main/preprints/A-Negative-Solution-to-the-Finite-Lattice-Representation-Problem-September-24-2026
Desired outcome: A specific upper bound like maybe n<=10^{10^10} with an understandable proof.

Title/name of problem: Classification of finite simple groups
Short description of problem (100 words: The CFSG is in principle a known theorem, but the proof is very long and I think partly disputed. The *statement* of the CFSG has been formalized in Lean. Is there an easier way to do it? Can large parts of it be formalized?
Reference/source material: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classification_of_finite_simple_groups
Desired outcome: Bring the CFSG in from the cold by formalizing large parts of it in Lean, or by finding a simplification in the proofs of the classification.

Title/name of problem: abc conjecture
Short description of problem (100 words: Mochizuki claims a proof of the abc conjecture, but the proof is complicated and not widely accepted. The very ambitious task is to contribute to a resolution of the situation by obtaining a brand new (AI-generated) idea.
Reference/source material: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abc_conjecture
Desired outcome: Any progress on this notorious problem would be of value.

Title/name of problem: NP-completeness of HP protein folding model
Short description of problem (100 words: Berger and Leighton (RECOMB 1998) and Papadimitriou et al. proved that optimality of an energy level in the hydrophobic-polar protein folding model has an NP-complete decision problem, in the 2D and 3D lattices. Can their complicated proofs be simplified?
Desired outcome: Ideally a formalized proof in Lean; alternatively, a simplification of the construction(s).

Title/name of problem: Weak factorization for the biholomorphic Hardy space
Short description of problem (100 words:
(Note: this is a shorted re-write of the original submission, which was long and mostly in LaTeX)

H^p(T^2) consists of L^p functions on the 2-torus whose Fourier coefficients vanish for negative indices (analytic functions in both variables). H^2 ⊙ H^2 is the "weak product": all H^1 functions expressible as infinite sums h = Σ f_j g_j (f_j, g_j ∈ H^2) with Σ ||f_j||_2 ||g_j||_2 < ∞.

The open weak factorization problem for the bidisc is whether the converse norm inequality holds: Can every H^1 function on the bidisc be factored this way with a uniform bound? Equivalently, are H^1(T^2) and H^2(T^2) ⊙ H^2(T^2) equal as normed spaces?

Currently we know H^2 ⊙ H^2 sits inside H^1 contractively. The open problem asks whether this containment reverses - whether ||h||{H^2⊙H^2} ≤ C||h||{H^1} for some constant C. This is the dual formulation of the bidisc Nehari problem.
Reference/source material: https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF02392840
Desired outcome: The answer to this problem and a new proof of the main theorem in the reference

Title/name of problem: Clustered Hadwiger's theorem
Short description of problem (100 words:
The Clustered Hadwiger's theorem, proved by Dujmović, Esperet, Morin and Wood asserts that for every positive integer $t$, every $K_t$-minor-free graph is $(t−1)$-colorable with monochromatic components of bounded size. 

The proof is complex and relies on Robertson-Seymour Graph Minor Structure theorem, which in turn has a proof spanning hundreds of pages. On the other hand, van den Heuvel and Wood gave an elegant ``book" proof of a weaker statement where $(t-1)$-colorability is replaced by $(2t-2)$-colorability.

The goal is to obtain a short proof of The Clustered Hadwiger's theorem that doesn't rely on Graph Minor Structure theorem.
Reference/source material:
The Clustered Hadwiger's theorem: https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.06224
van den Heuvel and Wood proof: https://arxiv.org/abs/1704.06536
Desired outcome: The main goal is to obtain an elegant, self-contained proof of the Clustered Hadwiger's theorem. A weaker outcome would be an improvement  of van den Heuvel and Wood bound, which retains a short proof. A stronger outcome would be a self-contained proof of a strengthening The Clustered Hadwiger's theorem to list-colorings.

Title/name of problem: well-posedness and stability of Landau equation, Vlasov-Landau equations and Boltzmann equation.
Short description of problem (100 words: well-posedness and stability of Landau equation, Vlasov-Landau equations and Boltzmann equation. Useful for nuclear fusion.

Title/name of problem: Mazur's Collatz Paper
Short description of problem (100 words: Recently, Mazur (using ChatGPT) proved that a positive proportion of positive integers iterate to 1 under the Collatz map, massively improving upon Tao's result. However, the paper is AI-generated and terribly written, so it would be valuable to understand this paper and perhaps rewrite it to be more conceptual.

https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/forum-of-mathematics-pi/article/almost-all-orbits-of-the-collatz-map-attain-almost-bounded-values/1008CC2DF91AF87F66D190C5E01C907F
Desired outcome: A human-readable paper which explains the ideas behind this new breakthrough. Preferably, a new way to phrase this argument which is more conceptually nice.

Title/name of problem: Topological group extensions and the cohomology of classifying spaces
Short description of problem (100 words:
Let G be a group and A be a G-module. My team will work on the problems of

1) extending the classical correspondence between G-equivariant Yoneda extensions of A and the cohomology of BG to the context of topological groups, and

2) extending the correspondence between group extensions of G by A and the second cohomology of BG to the context of topological groups.

Partial progress was made towards these results in my Master's thesis, and the purpose of the project will be to improve the methods and generalize the results as a byproduct.
Reference/source material:
Jain, P. (2025). Central Extensions of Topological Groups and the Cohomology of Classifying Spaces [Master's thesis, IISER, Pune]. IISER Pune Digital Repository. https://dr.iiserpune.ac.in/handle/123456789/10020
A copy can be downloaded here:
https://drive.google.com/file/d/1aLrZeLQ014gvvikD1G2gADeI3FxpJ5ea/view?usp=drivesdk

Jain, P., Joshi, R., Spallone, S. (2026). Central Extensions and Cohomology. arXiv preprint. arXiv:2307.14658
Desired outcome: My team aims to provide a clean exposition of the problem in a way which reduces all the ideas down to undergraduate mathematics + elementary algebraic topology (e.g. Hatcher's book). We plan on making the final artefact easy to navigate at various levels of detail (from a summary for experts to a detailed exposition for advanced undergrads).

Title/name of problem: Hassett divisors and the lattice-theoretic picture of cubic fourfold rationality
Short description of problem (100 words: A smooth cubic fourfold is special if it contains an algebraic surface not homologous to a complete intersection. Hassett showed these form a countable family of divisors C_d in the moduli space, nonempty iff d > 6 and d ≡ 0, 2 (mod 6), and that C_d has an associated K3 surface iff d is not divisible by 4, 9, or any odd prime ≡ 2 (mod 3). Intersections of these divisors are governed by lattice embeddings. The problem is to understand this lattice picture and its link to rationality.
Submitted Area: Algebraic geometry (Hodge theory and lattice theory; cubic fourfolds and K3 surfaces)
Reference/source material:
1. B. Hassett, “Special cubic fourfolds,” Compositio Mathematica 120 (2000), 1–23. See Theorem 1.0.1 (the divisors C_d; nonempty iff d > 6 and d ≡ 0, 2 mod 6) and Section 5 (associated K3 surfaces).

2. S. Yang and X. Yu, “On lattice polarizable cubic fourfolds,” arXiv:2103.09132. See Section 7, Algorithm 7.6 (irreducible components of C_{d₁} ∩ C_{d₂}) and Theorems 7.9 and 7.11 (worked examples C₂₀ ∩ C₃₈ and C₂₀ ∩ C₁₂).

3. S. Zucker, “The Hodge conjecture for cubic fourfolds,” Compositio Mathematica 34 (1977), 199–209. See Theorem 3.2.
Desired outcome: An open-source implementation of the algorithm for the irreducible components of intersections of two Hassett divisors, validated against published cases (for example, five components for C8 ∩ C14 and eight for C8 ∩ C26). Also an interactive visualization of the divisors and their intersections, and a written explainer connecting the lattice picture to K3 associations and rationality questions.

Title/name of problem: Positive Laurent phenomenon
Short description of problem (100 words: The notion of cluster algebras was motivated by understanding Lusztig's canonical basis (Item 1). This has led to spectacular mathematics, including Fomin and Zelevinsky's classification of cluster algebras by root systems (Item 2) and Gross-Hacking-Kell-Kontsevich's proof of positive structure constants for theta functions (Item 3) in cluster algebras. All three items come with quite sophisticated ideas and proofs, which most researchers that I know in the area are happy to assume without knowing too much about. I'd like to explore these
Submitted Area: Representation theory, algebraic combinatorics, mirror symmetry
Reference/source material:
Fomin-Zelevinsky: cluster algebras II, Inventiones Mathematicae (2003)
Gross-Hacking-Keel-Kontsevich: canonical bases for cluster algebras, JAMS (2018)
Desired outcome:
For the classification of cluster algebras: I'd like to see a more streamlined construction which explains why root systems enter and how the proof works
For scattering diagrams: I'd like to understand the rather difficult "induction on rank" argument that allows to reduce the general problem to the rank 2 problem

Title/name of problem: Kepler’s Theorem
Short description of problem (100 words: Kepler’s theorem states that the maximum density of a packing of identical spheres in three-dimensional Euclidean space is π/√18. Although proved and formally verified, its proof remains difficult to understand. The original proof relies on reducing the problem to a nonlinear optimization problem in ~150 variables.  The final solution involved numerically solving around 100,000 auxiliary linear optimization problems. Using modular forms, Maryna Viazovska provided a relatively short proof of the analogous problem in dimension 8 and---with several collaborators---in dimension 24. Can participants develop a clearer exposition of a significant part of the argument, or investigate how its geometric ideas extend to related packing problems? Possible directions include visualizing local density bounds and geometric decompositions, simplifying selected arguments, or exploring analogous questions in higher dimensions or constrained regions.
Submitted Area: Discrete geometry; sphere packing; computational geometry.
Reference/source material:
Thomas C. Hales, “A proof of the Kepler conjecture,” Annals of Mathematics 162 (2005), 1065–1185. Paper

Thomas Hales et al., “A formal proof of the Kepler conjecture,” Forum of Mathematics, Pi 5 (2017), e2. Paper
Desired outcome: A modified proof the Kepler conjecture with less reliance on numerical verification (e.g. reduction to a simpler optimization problem) or a structurally simpler proof of the conjecture using different techniques altogether in the spirit of Maryna Viazovska's work in 8 dimensions.

Title/name of problem: The Four-Color Theorem
Short description of problem (100 words:
An arbitrary map can be colored using four colors such that every two regions sharing a boundary receive distinct colors. In graph theory, it is equivalent to say every planar graph has a proper 4-coloring.

The Appel-Haken proof and later Robertson-Sanders-Seymour-Thomas proof rely on large computer-assisted case checks, and Gonthier formalized it in Coq (2005). Understanding and exposition remain hard. Is there a more conceptual route, for example via Kauffman’s or Tait-edge-coloring algebra, or a visualizable reducibility check?
Reference/source material:
K. Appel and W. Haken, Every Planar Map Is Four Colorable, A.M.S. Contemp. Math.
98 (1989).
N. Robertson, D. Sanders, P. Seymour, and R. Thomas, The four-colour theorem. J. Combin. Theory Ser. B 70 (1997), no. 1, 2--44.
(Robin Thomas's website) https://thomas.math.gatech.edu/FC/fourcolor.html 

Digestible overview: https://projecteuclid.org/journals/illinois-journal-of-mathematics/volume-60/issue-1/Wolfgang-Haken-and-the-four-color-problem/10.1215/ijm/1498032028.pdf

The 1976 Proof: https://projecteuclid.org/journals/illinois-journal-of-mathematics/volume-21/issue-3/Every-planar-map-is-four-colorable-Part-I-Discharging/10.1215/ijm/1256049011.pdf"

Gonthier's formalization: Gonthier, “Formal proof—the four-color theorem,” Notices of the AMS 55 (2008)
Desired outcome:
The current proofs reduce the problem to a finite case checking and then use computer assistance to finish the last steps. A preferable outcome would be a human-checkable proof, though it may still be hard even with AI-assistance. AI might be able to help find deep connections with other subjects such as algebra and topology. An illuminating alternative proof strategy will be very good.

A readable tour of the unavoidable-set and reducibility machinery with interactive tools, or an independent verification of selected components.

Title/name of problem: Hodge Modules
Short description of problem (100 words: Hodge Modules are created by Saito, concerning the most general form of decomposition theorem for projective direct image. But the original papers are hard to read, and very few people understand and use them. It would be good to have a better understanding or simplified proof.
Reference/source material: Morihiko Saito. Modules de Hodge Polarisables.

Title/name of problem: Positive rates
Short description of problem (100 words: The positive rates conjecture is/was a famous problem in probability and ergodic theory about random cellular automata. A counterexample was constructed by Gacs, but it is so complicated that perhaps no other person ever truly believed that it worked. The problem is philosophically interesting as it can be thought of in terms of whether perfect error correction is possible in distributed systems subject to noise— Gacs says yes!
Reference/source material: The main reference is Gacs “ Reliable Cellular Automata with Self-Organization”. See also “A Reader's Guide to Gacs's “Positive Rates” Paper“ by Gray.
Desired outcome: Since the correctness of Gacs argument is in doubt, a formal verification is genuinely desirable here. But more useful would be a simplification that can easily be understood and verified by hand.

Title/name of problem: Beyond Endoscopy for GL_2: Reconstruction, Simplification, and Verification of Existing Proofs
Short description of problem (100 words: Langlands’ Beyond Endoscopy program seeks to establish functoriality through the analytic properties of automorphic L-functions and trace formulas. Significant progress for GL_2 has been achieved through the work of Langlands, Venkatesh, Altug, and others. However, the existing proofs are technically demanding, scattered across multiple papers, and difficult to fully understand. This project aims to systematically reconstruct, summarize, simplify, and independently verify these proofs, potentially using AI-assisted tools. The ultimate goals are to develop a coherent, accessible exposition, discover more conceptual arguments, and identify techniques that may extend to higher-rank groups.
Submitted Area: Number Theory (Automorphic Forms and the Langlands Program), Representation Theory, and Harmonic Analysis.
Reference/source material:
1. R. P. Langlands, Beyond Endoscopy, in Contributions to Automorphic Forms, Geometry, and Number Theory, edited by H. Hida, D. Ramakrishnan, and F. Shahidi, Johns Hopkins University Press, 2004, pp. 611–697.

2. A. Venkatesh, Beyond Endoscopy and Special Forms on GL(2), Journal für die reine und angewandte Mathematik 577 (2004), 23–80. DOI:  ⁠10.1515/crll.2004.2004.577.23

3. S. Ali Altug, Beyond Endoscopy via the Trace Formula, Parts I–III:
* Part I: Poisson Summation and Isolation of Special Representations, Compositio Mathematica 151 (2015), no. 10, 1791–1820.
* Part II: Asymptotic Expansions of Fourier Transforms and Bounds Towards the Ramanujan Conjecture, American Journal of Mathematics 139 (2017), no. 4, 863–913.
* Part III: The Standard Representation, Journal of the Institute of Mathematics of Jussieu 19 (2020), no. 4, 1349–1387.
Desired outcome: A comprehensive, self-contained, and accessible exposition of the existing proofs of Beyond Endoscopy for GL(2), with a clear explanation of the main ideas, technical arguments, and logical dependencies. Participants should independently verify key steps, identify and resolve any gaps or ambiguities, and explore opportunities to simplify the proofs or develop more conceptual alternative arguments. AI-assisted mathematical reasoning and formal verification tools may be employed where appropriate. Ideally, the project will produce a polished mathematical manuscript, potentially accompanied by computational or formal verification resources, and identify promising directions for extending the methods to higher-rank groups.

Title/name of problem: Hoeffding's D Statistic
Short description of problem (100 words: In 1948 Hoeffding published his paper "A non-parametric test of independence" in which he defines a statistic ('D') and provides some examples of its computation. However, I have personally found the development of the statistic from this paper to be more than a bit confusing, and, given that it is frequently used in applied fields (especially biostatistics) I imagine there are many others who do not have a good intuitive understanding of what it measures. Furthermore, the null distribution of the D statistic is not well understood for all sample sizes (Hoeffding's paper provides explicit descriptions for n = 5,6,7 and an asymptotic description as n -> infinity, but this is not always applicable to researchers working with moderate data sets, such as those with 8 to 50 samples).
Reference/source material:
https://www.jstor.org/stable/2236021?seq=1 (Hoeffding's original paper)
https://academic.oup.com/bib/article/15/6/906/176706 (an example of the usage of this method in biostatistics/gene expression)
Desired outcome: An intuitive or more accessible description of the statistic, which could include a visualization of what the statistic measures/detects. A computation of the null distribution for 7 < n < infinity. Generalizations or improved connections/comparisons to other correlation metrics would also be useful.

Title/name of problem: Gaps in Spectral Gap Literature
Short description of problem (100 words: The first result in this area was an unreadable paper by Joel Friedman. Charles Bordenave wrote a more readable paper but it was still quite hard. Brito-Ioana-Harris wrote a yet more readable paper, but relied on a key lemma by Bordenave that they were unable to reprove in an intuitive way (Prop 28 in Bordenave's paper; Lemma 7 in B-I-H). (I haven't fully surveyed the field to see if there are newer papers that make this stuff clearer).
Submitted Area: Random graphs, random matrices, spectral gap
Reference/source material:
Brito-Ioana-Harris, 2021: https://arxiv.org/pdf/1804.07808
Bordenave, 2019: https://arxiv.org/pdf/1502.04482
Friedman, 2004: https://arxiv.org/pdf/cs/0405020
Friedman & Kohler, 2014: https://arxiv.org/pdf/1403.3462
Desired outcome: An intuitive proof of Proposition 28 in Bordenave's paper; a deeper exploration of these papers, intricacies and gaps between them, explanation and commentary/visualizations to help those learning the theory.

Title/name of problem: Compression as a Framework for Undecidability and Computational Complexity
Short description of problem (100 words: Compression is a recurring mechanism in undecidability proofs, including those for Wang tilings, MIP* = RE, and MIP^co = coRE. Abstract compression criteria characterize RE/coRE-completeness under suitable hypotheses, suggesting a reusable framework for understanding computational hardness. This project explores three directions: simplifying existing undecidability proofs through compression; finding new applications, potentially to quantum channel capacity; and developing analogous compression criteria for completeness at higher levels of the arithmetical hierarchy or for decidable complexity classes. The goal is to clarify what makes compression work and turn that understanding into more accessible proofs and new mathematical connections.
Reference/source material:
1. Andrew Marks, “A remark on compression,” lecture slides, October 19, 2023. Presents an abstract recursive compression lemma, its proof, and applications to Wang tilings and nonlocal games. Particularly relevant are the slides titled “Compression lemma,” “Proof,” and “Open problems/requests.”
https://sfo3.digitaloceanspaces.com/slmath-production-assets/system/paperclip/documents/data/000/097/705/original/AM.pdf

2. Junqiao Lin, “MIPᶜᵒ = coRE” (2025), arXiv:2510.07162. See §1.1.1 and §4, especially Definitions 4.1 and 4.3 and Theorems 4.4–4.5, for compression conditions characterizing RE/coRE-completeness under the stated hypotheses.
https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.07162

3. Hamoon Mousavi, Seyed Sajjad Nezhadi, and Henry Yuen, “Nonlocal Games, Compression Theorems, and the Arithmetical Hierarchy,” STOC 2022, pp. 1–11; arXiv:2110.04651. Develops gapless compression and establishes Π₂⁰-completeness of deciding whether a nonlocal game’s quantum value equals one, providing a concrete starting point for exploring higher-level compression criteria.
https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.04651
Desired outcome:
Participants should develop a clearer understanding of compression as a reusable method for proving computational hardness. Teams may pursue one or more of three directions:

1. Simplify existing proofs. Reconstruct a known undecidability proof using an abstract compression lemma, separating the problem-specific construction from the general recursion argument. Identify opportunities to weaken hypotheses, streamline the construction, or explain connections between different proofs.

2. Explore new applications. Investigate compression procedures for other mathematical problems. Ordinary quantum channel capacity is an ambitious candidate; a valuable intermediate outcome would be a precisely formulated decision problem and a conditional undecidability proof identifying the missing compression lemma.

3. Extend completeness characterizations. Seek analogues of the RE/coRE compression criteria for higher levels of the arithmetical hierarchy, beginning with Σ₂⁰ or Π₂⁰, or for selected decidable complexity classes. The aim is to identify useful necessary-and-sufficient conditions, including quantitative requirements, rather than merely restating completeness in different language.

Deliverables could include a self-contained exposition with worked examples, a simplified or formalized proof, a new compression theorem, or a rigorous obstruction to a proposed extension. Teams need not resolve a new open problem: a substantial improvement in understanding an existing result would be a successful contribution.

Title/name of problem: Finite-time blowup for the forced three-dimensional incompressible Navier–Stokes equations
Short description of problem (100 words: In September 2026 OpenAI reported a proof that for every positive viscosity there exist smooth initial data and smooth forcing for which the 3D incompressible Navier–Stokes equations have no global smooth solution. The AI-authored write-up is long and its Lean 4 formalization checks the result without explaining it. The open question is the mechanism: what the forcing does and how the construction sits beside the forced blow-up constructions of Córdoba and Martínez-Zoroa, the Caffarelli–Kohn–Nirenberg partial regularity theory, the Escauriaza–Seregin–Šverák criterion, and Tao's averaged equation.
Submitted Area: Analysis of PDEs (primary); fluid dynamics; mathematical formalization in Lean 4
Reference/source material: (1) OpenAI, NavierStokesAndEuler: Lean 4 formalization of finite-time blowup for the forced Navier–Stokes equations on R^3 and the periodic torus, https://github.com/openai/NavierStokesAndEuler (2026). (2) D. Córdoba, L. Martínez-Zoroa and F. Zheng, "Finite time blow-up for the hypodissipative Navier Stokes equations with a force in L^1_t C^{1,ε}_x ∩ L^∞_t L^2_x", arXiv:2407.06776 (2024). (3) L. Caffarelli, R. Kohn and L. Nirenberg, "Partial regularity of suitable weak solutions of the Navier–Stokes equations", Comm. Pure Appl. Math. 35 (1982), 771–831.
Desired outcome: A human-readable account of the blowup construction that identifies the mechanism and the role of the forcing, ties each step to the Lean declaration that proves it, and situates the result against the partial regularity theory and earlier forced blow-up constructions, together with its physical relevance for fluid dynamics.

Title/name of problem: Proving the Gaussian correlation inequality
Short description of problem (100 words: The Gaussian correlation inequality is a famous inequality in mathematical statistics. The inequality was conjectured in 1955 and proved in 2014.
Reference/source material: https://arxiv.org/abs/1512.08776
Desired outcome:
The first proof was constructed using probabilistic arguments, but perhaps it is possible to construct a more intuitive and concise geometric proof of the inequality. As this Quanta article below shows, it has a nice geometric interpretation.
https://www.quantamagazine.org/statistician-proves-gaussian-correlation-inequality-20170328/

Title/name of problem: Planar Halving Lines
Short description of problem (100 words: We are given n points in the plane. A pair of points is a halving pair if its line (a halving line) leaves (n-2)/2 points on either side. How many halving lines are possible?
Reference/source material:
1. Tamal Dey's longstanding bound appears in: "Improved Bounds for Planar k -Sets and Related Problems." https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/PL00009354.pdf
2. A recent improvement on the bound from OpenAI: https://github.com/openai/math/blob/main/preprints/A-power-saving-for-planar-halving-lines-September-25-2026/main.pdf
3. An open problems page describing the problem: https://jeffe.cs.illinois.edu/open/ksets.html
Desired outcome: As with many of the results in the recent OpenAI "drop", this improvement on the longstanding bound is difficult to decipher. Historically, arguments giving increasingly tight bounds for the problem have used a dual formulation and argued about arrangements of lines, and the recent proof also appears to do this. At minimum, the new results/techniques should be nicely visualizable. It would be quite a nice project to visualize the new techniques via this dual setup, and understand how precisely the new bound is obtained. Perhaps it might give us new ideas to improve bounds in combinatorial geometry more broadly.

Title/name of problem: Kuroda’s Class Number Formula and  Correcting the Computation of Unit Indices
Short description of problem (100 words: We will revisit Charkani’s restriction on the possible values of Leopoldt’s unit index in totally real cyclic fields of degree pq. This restriction does not hold in full generality, and we aim to explain why, establish corrected bounds, and examine the consequences for the associated class-number statements. We will also discuss Lemmermeyer’s correction to Walter’s generalization of Kuroda’s class-number formula. The comparison will distinguish two separate issues: accounting for roots of unity in products of subfield unit groups, and understanding why a rational character decomposition need not give an integral decomposition of the unit lattice
Reference/source material:
1. M. E. Charkani, “On Leopoldt’s Index and Relative Class Number of a Real Cyclic Extension,” preprint, 1997.

2. F. Lemmermeyer, “Kuroda’s Class Number Formula,” *Acta Arithmetica* **66**, no. 3 (1994), 245–260.

3. H. W. Leopoldt, “Über Einheitengruppe und Klassenzahl reeller abelscher Zahlkörper,” *Abhandlungen der Deutschen Akademie der Wissenschaften zu Berlin*, Klasse für Mathematik und Allgemeine Naturwissenschaften, Jahrgang 1953, Nr. 2 (1954). Also submitted as a doctoral dissertation, University of Hamburg, 1954. (there is a french review on this)
Desired outcome:
Our goal is to give a clear account of the unit-index problem for totally real cyclic number fields of degree pq, where p and q are distinct primes. We will revisit the four-value restriction stated in Charkani’s work, which does not hold in full generality, and establish a corrected statement with a detailed proof. We want to explain where the additional possibilities come from, how the factorization of cyclotomic polynomials over finite fields constrains the possible indices, and under which additional assumptions the original four-value conclusion holds.

We will include an explicit number-field counterexample and a calculation of its unit index that can be checked independently. We will also examine the class-number arguments that rely on the restriction to determine which conclusions remain valid and which need to be revised. In doing so, we will distinguish the restriction itself from the underlying class-number identities, which may remain valid.

To put this problem in context, we will discuss Lemmermeyer’s correction to Walter’s 1979 generalization of Kuroda’s class-number formula. The two issues arise for different reasons: one concerns roots of unity in products of subfield unit groups, while the other concerns the integral structure of the unit lattice, which is not fully captured by its rational character decomposition. Through worked examples, we will explain where these factors enter the calculations and how to account for them.

The intended outcome is a self-contained exposition, supported by examples and reproducible code. We will check the literature carefully, acknowledge the existing work, and distinguish known results from any new contributions. If time permits, we will also investigate which of the indices allowed by the corrected bounds actually occur for number fields.

Title/name of problem: Categorical groups and homotopy types
Short description of problem (100 words: Loday’s theorem states that cat^n-groups (equivalently, crossed n-cubes) model pointed connected homotopy (n+1)-types. The original 1982 proof had gaps; complete proofs were later given by Porter (via simplicial groups) and by Bullejos–Cegarra–Duskin (via multisimplicial groups). Even the corrected proofs are hard to follow: the delicate steps are the exactness of nerves of cat^n-groups under iterated fiber products and the verification of the hypotheses of the Bousfield–Friedlander theorem. No formalization exists, and no exposition of the n=2 case is accessible to non-specialists.
Reference/source material: J.-L. Loday, “Spaces with finitely many non-trivial homotopy groups,” J. Pure Appl. Algebra 24 (1982), 179–202;  T. Porter, “n-types of simplicial groups and crossed n-cubes,” Topology 32 (1993), 5–24;  M. Bullejos, A. M. Cegarra, J. Duskin, “On cat^n-groups and homotopy types,” J. Pure Appl. Algebra 86 (1993), 135–154
Desired outcome: A Lean formalization of the n=1 case: crossed modules, cat^1-groups, their equivalence, and the equivalence of the resulting homotopy category with pointed connected 2-types. (b) A self-contained, illustrated exposition of the n=2 case (crossed squares and 3-types), with explicit treatment of the two delicate steps above and worked examples such as the crossed square of a pair of normal subgroups. A stretch goal is a sketch of how the general-n proof reduces to these two steps.

Title/name of problem: Jacquet-Langlands correspondence for GL(2)
Short description of problem (100 words: The Jacquet–Langlands correspondence, established by Hervé Jacquet and Robert Langlands in 1970, is a foundational result in number theory and representation theory. It links automorphic representations of GL(2) with those of the multiplicative group of a quaternion algebra, matching representations that share the same local data and L-functions. As one of the earliest proven cases of Langlands functoriality, it became an essential tool in modern arithmetic, including work leading to the proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem.
Reference/source material:
Jacquet, H.; Langlands, Robert P. (1970), Automorphic Forms on GL(2), Lecture Notes in Mathematics, vol. 114, Berlin, New York: Springer-Verlag, doi:10.1007/BFb0058988, ISBN 978-3-540-04903-6, MR 0401654

If early attempts to a new approach bear no fruit, we could aim at a LEAN formalization of the trace formula proof, with an accompanying human-readable mathematically consistent writeup.

Title/name of problem: Quantitative Onset and Nonlinear Evolution of Tollmien–Schlichting Instabilities in Navier–Stokes Flows
Short description of problem (100 words: This project investigates whether analytical methods from Navier–Stokes regularity theory can quantitatively characterize the onset and nonlinear evolution of Tollmien–Schlichting instabilities in viscous shear flows. Using the Orr–Sommerfeld equation, spectral analysis, and perturbative energy estimates, participants will study Reynolds-number-dependent instability thresholds, disturbance growth rates, and nonlinear interactions. The project aims to connect rigorous PDE stability and instability estimates with the early stages of boundary-layer transition, distinguishing the onset of unstable modes from the development of sustained turbulence.
Submitted Area: Partial Differential Equations, Mathematical Fluid Dynamics, Hydrodynamic Stability, Spectral Theory, and Nonlinear Analysis
Desired outcome: Participants will derive the perturbation equations for a selected laminar flow and establish or reproduce nonlinear energy estimates that quantify how stability depends on Reynolds number and perturbation amplitude. The project aims to obtain a rigorous stability bound, investigate transient growth, and compare theoretical thresholds with known transition behavior. A final report will explain the analytical methods, assumptions, and limitations of the resulting predictions.

Title/name of problem: Low-memory structure of Nesterov-like acceleration  (I made this title)
Short description of problem (100 words: Can additional memory improve the optimal performance of first-order optimization methods? For a specified class of objectives and a fixed gradient-query budget, compare methods maintaining an iterate and one auxiliary vector with methods allowed a second auxiliary vector. The goal is to identify settings in which the latter achieve a strictly better finite-horizon minimax guarantee, or prove that the additional state cannot help. In the latter case, seek a common structural explanation across various settings. To make the comparison precise, restrict both families to linear first-order updates with predetermined scalar coefficients and specify the performance criterion.
Reference/source material:
primary reference
d’Aspremont, Alexandre, Damien Scieur, and Adrien Taylor. "Acceleration methods." Foundations and trends in optimization 5.1-2 (2021): 1-245., Chapter 4. Nesterov Acceleration

methodology related
Das Gupta, Shuvomoy, Bart PG Van Parys, and Ernest K. Ryu. "Branch-and-bound performance estimation programming: a unified methodology for constructing optimal optimization methods: S. Das Gupta et al." Mathematical Programming 204.1 (2024): 567-639.
Desired outcome:
For basic settings like convex quadratics or L-smooth convex functions, it is known that additional memory cannot improve the worst-case performance. The participant will figure this out by combining literatures.

A small contribution can start from experimenting new algorithms (by finding extremal methods) for other problem settings, using the BnB-PEP or our AutoOPT framework. This can be parallelized for various interpolation conditions given plenty computational resources. One could also try characterization of the lower bound functions for the various settings. By studying these individual cases, one can hopefully identify a common structure that makes the statement false. (This is the ultimate question, but I don't expect this solved in Mathathon)

Aside from the main problem, another possible direction could be to investigate why momentum acceleration works for more practical non-convex settings. One can also work on the continuous-time analysis (based on Su-Boyd-Candes result), or connection to classical physics by interpreting the states (x, p) in the phase space (i.e. presymplectic discretization) depending on their interests.

Title/name of problem: Hadwiger-Nelson Problem - The Euclidean plane is not five-colorable

Since 1950 it has been known to be 4, 5, 6 or 7. De Grey (2018) showed it is at least 5. OpenAI recently proved that five colors are insufficient, leaving six or seven as possibilities. An unexpected ingredient is a transfer theorem: a proper k-coloring exists if and only if a measurable k-coloring exists that avoids monochromatic unit-distance pairs almost everywhere. Title/name of problem: Monstrous moonshine

Title/name of problem: Asymptotic Growth of Integer Partitions into Powers
Short description of problem (100 words:
Let \(P_{k,r}(n)\) denote the number of partitions of an integer \(n\) into \(k\)-th powers, with each part appearing at most \(r\) times. The generating function is

\[
\prod_{j=1}^{\infty}\frac{1-q^{(r+1)j^k}}{1-q^{j^k}}.
\]

The central problem is to determine how multiplicity restrictions affect the asymptotic growth of \(P_{k,r}(n)\) relative to unrestricted partitions. Of particular interest are explicit asymptotic formulas, higher-order correction terms, and rigorous error bounds describing the accuracy and convergence rates of these approximations.
Submitted Area: Analytic Number Theory, Enumerative Combinatorics, Asymptotic Analysis
Reference/source material:
E. M. Wright, “Asymptotic Partition Formulae. III. Partitions into k-th Powers,” Acta Mathematica, 63 (1934), 143–191.
https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02547353

K. F. Roth and G. Szekeres, “Some Asymptotic Formulae in the Theory of Partitions,” The Quarterly Journal of Mathematics, 5 (1954), 241–259.
https://doi.org/10.1093/qmath/5.1.241

Cormac O'Sullivan, “Detailed Asymptotic Expansions for Partitions into Powers,” arXiv:2205.13468 (2022; revised 2023).
https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.13468
Desired outcome: A rigorous derivation of the asymptotic relationship between restricted and unrestricted partitions into \(k\)-th powers, ideally including an explicit asymptotic formula with higher-order correction terms and effective error bounds. Of particular interest are quantitative estimates for the convergence rate, improvements in approximation accuracy, and a generalization across different powers \(k\) and multiplicity restrictions \(r\). A computational comparison between theoretical approximations and exact partition counts would help illustrate the results.

Title/name of problem: Probabilistic and Asymptotic Approaches to the Hook-Length Formula for Young Tableaux

Title/name of problem: SLn P=W Conjecture via endoscopy

Since 2022, it has been proved in three ways: by Maulik-Shen, by Hausel-Mellit-Minets-Schiffmann, and by Maulik-Shen-Yin. The P=W Conjecture has an SLn variant, which is proved by OpenAI in Oct 2026. Title/name of problem: Understanding a Proposed Counterexample to Reduced Baum–Connes Injectivity
Short description of problem (100 words: The Baum–Connes conjecture predicts that the assembly map, which relates the topology of a group to the K-theory of its reduced group C*-algebra, is an isomorphism. A recent manuscript released by OpenAI claims to construct a finitely generated torsion-free group for which the coefficient-free reduced assembly map fails to be rationally injective, providing a counterexample to the conjecture. This project would examine the proposed proof, explain its main ideas and connection to index theory, and clarify the significance of the claimed counterexample.
Submitted Area: Noncommutative geometry; operator algebras; K-theory and index theory; geometric group theory.
Reference/source material:
1. “A torsion-free counterexample to reduced Baum–Connes injectivity,” manuscript dated September 23, 2026, released in OpenAI’s mathematics collection. This is the main text to be studied; its introduction states the claimed result and outlines the construction.

Desired outcome:
A clear and mathematically careful exposition of the proposed counterexample, aimed at graduate students with some background in operator algebras, topology, or index theory. Participants would explain the assembly map and the significance of injectivity, reconstruct the main steps of the proposed proof, and clarify how the geometric and analytic parts of the construction fit together.

The exposition should distinguish arguments that have been independently checked from steps that remain unresolved, and develop simpler or alternative explanations where possible. The final project could consist of expository notes and a presentation that make the manuscript more accessible and provide a useful basis for further examination of its claims.

Title/name of problem: Hylland's random dictatorship theorem for cardinal preferences
Short description of problem (100 words: Arrow (1951), Gibbard (1973) and Satterthwaite (1975) showed that with at least three alternatives, natural conditions on aggregating or eliciting ordinal preferences force dictatorship. Hylland (1980) proved a version for lotteries and von Neumann-Morgenstern utilities: with finitely many voters and alternatives (at least three), every strategy-proof rule mapping all utility profiles to lotteries, which gives a unanimously top-ranked alternative probability 1 and a unanimously bottom-ranked alternative probability 0, is a random dictatorship. Dutta, Peters and Sen (2007) proposed a simpler proof using only the top condition; their 2008 erratum finds a gap and closes it only under an extra assumption.
Submitted Area: Game theory: mathematical social choice and mechanism design
Reference/source material:
1. A. Hylland, Strategy proofness of voting procedures with lotteries as outcomes and infinite sets of strategies, unpublished paper, 1980.
2. B. Dutta, H. Peters and A. Sen, Strategy-proof cardinal decision schemes, Social Choice and Welfare 28 (2007), 163-179, doi:10.1007/s00355-006-0152-9; erratum, Social Choice and Welfare 30 (2008), 701-702, doi:10.1007/s00355-008-0299-7.
3. S. Nandeibam, The structure of decision schemes with cardinal preferences, Review of Economic Design 17 (2013), 205-238, doi:10.1007/s10058-012-0130-x.
Desired outcome: A new geometric argument for Hylland's theorem and nice visualizations of this important result, together with a short, transparent exposition.

Title/name of problem: The Quasi-Riemann Hypothesis
Short description of problem (100 words: The Riemann hypothesis conjectures that all nontrivial zeros of the Riemann zeta function have real part 1/2. A quasi-Riemann hypothesis is a weaker version of this conjecture, a zero-free half-plane of the form Re(s)>sigma, for some sigma < 1. Last month, OpenAI published two papers establishing quasi-Riemann, one asserting a zero-free region Re(s)>11/12 and the other a zero-free region Re(s)>7/8. Much of the proof is implicitly operating in the realm of Tate's Thesis, and subsequent extensions to Dedekind Zeta Functions by AxiomMath further solidify these connections.
Reference/source material:
https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-1-4757-3085-2
https://github.com/openai/math/blob/main/preprints/The-Quasi-Riemann-Hypothesis-September-30-2026/paper.pdf

 https://github.com/openai/math/blob/main/preprints/The-Quasi-Riemann-Hypothesis-October-5-2026/paper2.pdf
Desired outcome:
Mathematicians have been expending great effort to understand the October 5 Quasi-RH paper, which establishes a zero-free half-plane Re(s)>11/12. This paper was written with human assistance and is more digestible than the much longer September 30 paper, which obtains the stronger zero-free half-plane Re(s)>7/8. I hope that participants can simplify and provide better exposition of this nearly 200-page proof, showcasing its key techniques and limitations.

Another goal is a shortened exposition of a proof of quasi-GRH, with extensions to Hecke L-functions or identified obstructions to these extensions. Explicit separation of purely analytic inputs and adelic machinery, trying to minimize these analytic inputs.

Title/name of problem: Gromov's Simplicial Volume Vanishing Conjecture

Gromov conjectured that if a closed manifold admits a Riemannian metric with positive scalar curvature, then its simplicial volume must vanish. The problem hopes to establish a relationship between a topological quantity (the simplicial volume) and a geometric quantity (scalar curvature). Title/name of problem: Yau's conjecture
Short description of problem (100 words: Yau’s conjecture predicts that the nodal set of a Laplace eigenfunction with eigenvalue λ on a closed smooth manifold has measure comparable to √λ. In September 2026, AI-generated preprints claimed the upper bound on smooth surfaces and counterexamples in dimensions 3–5. These ~120 pages are hard to read and not yet confirmed by experts. We explain them around one question: why does dimension 2 differ from dimension ≥3? The same dichotomy appears for Landis’ conjecture. We will relate the AI arguments to prior human work, identifying what the AI added, and isolate the new idea in the 2D proof.
Submitted Area: Analysis of PDE, spectral geometry, differential geometry, harmonic analysis — specifically: nodal sets of Laplace eigenfunctions and unique continuation
Reference/source material:
1. A. Logunov and E. Malinnikova, “Review of Yau’s conjecture on zero sets of Laplace eigenfunctions”, Current Developments in Mathematics 2018, International Press. arXiv:1908.01639.
2. “Sharp nodal length on smooth surfaces”, preprint, September 23, 2026. https://github.com/openai/math/blob/main/preprints/Sharp-nodal-length-on-smooth-surfaces-September-23-2026/paper.pdf
3. “Smooth counterexamples to Yau’s nodal upper bound in dimensions three and four”, preprint, September 23, 2026. https://github.com/openai/math/blob/main/preprints/Smooth-counterexamples-to-Yaus-nodal-upper-bound-in-dimensions-three-and-four-September-23-2026/paper.pdf
Desired outcome:
A readable account of what the AI-generated arguments actually do, aimed at mathematicians outside the immediate specialty. Concretely:

A clear outline of the counterexample in dimensions ≥3: its main steps, which ones are standard and which are new, and why the construction does not work on surfaces.
An identification of the key new ingredient in the 2D proof, compared with earlier approaches (doubling index, Carleman estimates) that reached weaker bounds.
A map of prior human work: which ideas were already available in the literature, including the analogous dimension-2 vs ≥3 dichotomy for Landis’ conjecture, and what exactly the AI contributed beyond them.
Visualizations that make the mechanism tangible: nodal sets of the constructed eigenfunctions compared with typical (random-wave) eigenfunctions, and the growth of nodal measure relative to √λ.

Title/name of problem: The power saving for planar unit distances

Reference/source material: (1) OpenAI, A power saving for planar unit distances (23 September 2026), https://github.com/openai/math/tree/main/preprints/A-power-saving-for-planar-unit-distances-September-23-2026 (2) J. Székely, Crossing numbers and hard Erdős problems in discrete geometry, Combin. Probab. Comput. 6 (1997), 353–358.
Desired outcome: A human-readable account of the proof's architecture, a clear explanation of exactly where it uses Euclidean structure and fails for Valtr's metric, and an explicit delta in the power saving.

Title/name of problem: Sorting Networks in O(log(n)) Depth
Short description of problem (100 words: Sorting lists is a fundamental problem in computer science that famously requires roughly n log(n) steps to do. However, this is only if the steps are taken sequentially; more efficient algorithms are possible if the steps are allowed to take place in parallel. A result of Ajtai-Komlós-Szemerédi shows that it is in fact possible to sort in O(log(n)) parallel rounds of operations. However, this algorithm (referred to as a sorting network) is famously difficult to understand and also impractical to implement. A simpler construction of these networks that have reasonable bounds on their depth would be of great interest in both theory and practice.
Reference/source material: https://dl.acm.org/doi/abs/10.1145/800061.808726, https://users.encs.concordia.ca/~chvatal/notes/aks.pdf, Volume 3 (Sorting and Searching) of The Art of Computer Programming
Desired outcome: A simplified construction of a O(log(n)) depth sorting network (simplified e.g. by making use of nicer algebraic gadgets to abstract out some of the complexity, or else a simplified explanation of the AKS construction). A sorting network that is practically implementable would be desirable, though not necessary

Title/name of problem: Rigidity of enumeration degrees
Short description of problem (100 words: OpenAI recently proved (in Lean) that the Turing degrees D_T are rigid. It is also known that the Turing degrees are definable in the enumeration degrees D_e, so that it follows that the enumeration degrees are rigid. But the definition of D_T in D_e is complicated, so it is not easy to obtain rigidity of D_e in Lean. The task is to find an easier way.
Reference/source material:
Cai, Ganchev, Lempp, Miller and Soskova (JAMS 2016)
https://github.com/openai/math/tree/main/preprints/Rigidity-of-the-Turing-degrees-September-24-2026

Title/name of problem: Tight Dimension Dependence for Convex Bandits
Short description of problem (100 words: The current state of art in the convex bandit problem, where a learner is tasked with optimising an unseen convex function with zero-order and noisy evaluations, is a regret bound of O(d^{2.5}\sqrt{n}), with d the dimension and n the number of data points. More recently, a lower bound of \Omega(d^{4/3}\sqrt{n}) was shown. Little is known on how this gap could be closed.
Reference/source material: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2607.18652 https://arxiv.org/pdf/2402.06535  https://arxiv.org/pdf/2406.06506

Title/name of problem: Hilbert’s tenth problem over the rationals
Short description of problem (100 words: Does an algorithm which determines whether an integer-coefficient polynomial in an arbitrary number of variables has a rational zero exist? This problem was recently resolved by OpenAI.

Title/name of problem: Non-uniqueness or uniqueness of Glimm-Lax solutions
Short description of problem (100 words: In hyperbolic conservation laws, the uniqueness or non-uniqueness of Glimm-Lax solutions has been open since they were first constructed 50 years ago. I have proven in recent work that all Sobolev data is unique AND I have a slop proof which shows uniqueness for ALL small L^\infty solutions outside a meagre set. We would like to understand and simplify our slop proof, and possibly extend it.

Title/name of problem: Inviscid limit for 1-d compressible MHD
Short description of problem (100 words: For hyperbolic systems in 1-D, we know the inviscid limit holds for small data, for general systems, and recent work by my team member Geng Chen has shown that the inviscid limit holds for the Navier-Stokes to Euler in the isentropic case. These two proofs are not obviously compatible. Title/name of problem: Taxonomizing mathematics: an exploration with minimal surfaces
Short description of problem (100 words: Develop a framework for organizing mathematical objects and existing results for human and machine exploration. Using minimal surfaces as an initial test case, we propose to: (1) consolidate known examples, constructions, and theorems; (2) encode geometric invariants, hypotheses, conclusions, and relationships in a machine-readable form designed for computational efficiency; (3) analyze the resulting data to uncover subtle connections and patterns across the literature; and (4) build interactive software enabling mathematicians to explore these structures. Periodic minimal surfaces, with their rich lattice symmetries and topology, offer a further example. The central objective is deeper human understanding through computational exploration.
Reference/source material: Meeks, W. H. III, and Rosenberg, H. (2005). “The uniqueness of the helicoid.” Annals of Mathematics, 161(2), 727–758; raizet, M. (2008). “On the genus of triply periodic minimal surfaces.” Journal of Differential Geometry, 79(2), 243–275; Meeks, W. H. III (1990). “The theory of triply periodic minimal surfaces.” Indiana University Mathematics Journal, 39(3), 877–936.
Desired outcome:
Interactive software and a data set that can be used for human exploration and understanding

This problem is not necessarily tied to minimal surfaces. Other geometric objects could be considered.

Title/name of problem: Dissecting OpenAI’s counterexamples to the Auslander-Reiten and Second Tachikawa conjecture for finite-dimensional algebras
Short description of problem (100 words:
The Auslander-Reiten and the Second Tachikawa conjectures belong to a web of homological conjectures which have strong influence on the development of the representation theory of finite-dimensional algebras for decades. Recently, OpenAI gave an intricate multi-step construction of rather special counterexamples, which are yet neither digested nor canonicalized. This project aims to verify key arguments, understand the underlying mechanisms, and seek simpler, more conceptual constructions. Guiding questions are whether these counterexamples are isolated phenomena or instances of a broader family, and where the mathematical novelty of the AI-generated constructions lies.

Tachikawa's second conjecture: Let A be a finite-dimensional self-injective algebra over a field k, and let M be a finitely generated A-module. Prove: if M has no nontrivial self-extensions in any positive degree, then M must be projective. In other words, if Ext^i_A(M, M) = 0 for every i > 0, then M is projective.
Submitted Area: Representation theory of finite-dimensional algebras, homological algebra, category theory, ring theory
Reference/source material:
Short formulations of the two conjectures can be found in the recent preprint, bottom of page 1 and top of page 2: 
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2609.19172 
This preprint establishes that both conjectures are equivalent.
(This preprint uses the slightly more general setup of Artin algebras instead of finite-dimensional algebras).

The counterexamples to these conjectures have been uploaded by OpenAI on October, 6th:
https://github.com/openai/math/blob/main/preprints/An-explicit-counterexample-to-the-Auslander-Reiten-conjecture-September-23-2026/paper.pdf 
https://github.com/openai/math/blob/main/preprints/A-counterexample-to-Tachikawas-second-conjecture-September-23-2026/paper.pdf

Both preprints are variations on the same construction pipeline. I include both to offer participants different ways to engage with the material.

Shortly thereafter, an AI-assisted, and generalized exposition appeared by Qiyue Tang:
https://hexagonmath.org/2610.00143v1

For the sake of completeness, here are the original references of the conjectures by Auslander-Reiten, and Tachikawa:
https://www.jstor.org/stable/2040102?seq=1
https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/BFb0059997
Desired outcome:
The primary outcome would be a self-contained, accessible exposition of the construction pipeline, verifying key arguments, explaining the fundamental ideas, and identifying precedents in the literature. This account should clarify which ingredients are essential and where simplifications or generalizations are possible. More ambitious goals include finding new, simpler counterexamples and interpreting the constructions through derived noncommutative algebraic geometry.

I would like to understand OpenAI's proposed counterexample to Tachikawa's Second Conjecture from both a ring-theoretic and a categorical perspective.

In particular:

1. How is the counterexample constructed in terms of the structure of the finite-dimensional self-injective algebra A and the module M? What ring-theoretic intuition allow all higher self-extension groups Ext^i_A(M, M) to vanish while M remains nonprojective?

2. Can you connect OpenAI's counterexample to the setting of a stable module category of A, an object with no positive-degree self-extensions M, and the zero object.

Title/name of problem: A Simpler Counterexample to Hadwiger's Conjecture
Short description of problem (100 words: Hadwiger's conjecture states that every graph with chromatic number at least k contains a K_k minor. OpenAI released a counterexample in its October 6, 2026 proof dump. The problem is to simplify the counterexample and its proof.
Reference/source material: https://github.com/openai/math/blob/main/preprints/A-counterexample-to-Hadwigers-conjecture-September-23-2026/paper.pdf
Desired outcome: A simpler construction of a counterexample to Hadwiger's conjecture, ideally with a shorter and more elementary proof.

Title/name of problem: Simplifying the Disproof of the Exponential Time Hypothesis
Short description of problem (100 words:
A 3-SAT problem consists of a long list of logic conditions joined together. To solve the puzzle, you must find a way to assign a value of TRUE or FALSE to every variable so that the entire formula evaluates to TRUE.

It was previously widely expected that such an algorithm did not exist: 3-SAT is the prototypical NP-complete problem, and a strengthening of P≠NP, the Exponential Time Hypothesis, asserted that there should be no “free-lunch” universally applicable trick for speeding up such a general problem, beyond constant multiplicative repackagings of the input (corresponding to lowering the base of the exponent).

These have been proven to be NP-complete (so if they are solvable efficiently, then P=NP). The Exponential Time Hypothesis (ETH) states that 3-SAT cannot be solved in subexponential time. In October 2026, OpenAI and Anthropic independently released claimed disproofs of ETH, each providing a subexponential-time algorithm. The problem is to simplify these proofs.
Submitted Area: Computational complexity theory, theoretical computer science
Reference/source material:
OpenAI: https://github.com/openai/math/blob/main/preprints/The-Exponential-Time-Hypothesis-is-False-October-25-2026/paper.pdf

Anthropic: https://github.com/anthropics/formal-math/blob/main/eth/paper.pdf
Desired outcome:
A simpler disproof of the Exponential Time Hypothesis, ideally with a shorter and more elementary argument.

Both papers contain unexpected moves enabling their unprecedented results. There is an extensive literature furnishing varied frameworks from which to view the SAT problem. It would thus be helpful to human understanding to recast the unexpected moves of these LLM-generated papers in the existing frameworks of human mathematicians.

Title/name of problem: Simplifying the Proof of Barnette's Conjecture

Title/name of problem: Simplifying the Proof of Seymour's Second-Neighborhood Conjecture
Short description of problem (100 words: Seymour's second-neighborhood conjecture states that every oriented graph has a vertex with at least as many second out-neighbors as first out-neighbors. OpenAI released a proof in its October 6, 2026 proof dump. The problem is to simplify this proof.

Title/name of problem: Digesting openAI's claimed proof of Bloch's conjecture
Short description of problem (100 words: Bloch's conjecture predicts that for a smooth connected projective complex surface X with geometric genus p_g(X) = 0, the Albanese homomorphism on degree-zero zero-cycles CH_0(X)_{deg=0} -> Alb(X) is an isomorphism.

For problem and background: Bloch's 'Lectures on Algebraic Cycles'

Desired outcome: Carefully digest and verify the AI-generated proof of Bloch's conjecture. For example, participants can give an exposition for the main strategy of the proof, and check whether the steps hold rigorously or contain subtle gaps. They can optionally formalize key lemmas in Lean. Participants can compare the approach to classical methods, identify which parts of the proof uses existing techniques, and which parts provides new techniques. Finally, they can provide some comments on whether the new techniques are helpful for proving higher dimensional analogs of Bloch's conjecture beyond surfaces.

Title/name of problem: Gigli’s characterization of Alexandrov curvature
Short description of problem (100 words: Gigli gave a notion of distributional curvature of a metric space.  OpenAI proved that (under the condition that the space is $RCD$) a metric space is Alexandrov (has sectional curvature bounded below by $k$ in the sense of triangular comparison) if and only if Gigli's distributional curvature is bounded below by $k$.
Reference/source material: https://github.com/openai/math/blob/main/preprints/Giglis-distributional-curvature-characterization-of-Alexandrov-spaces-September-24-2026/main.pdf
Desired outcome: The goal is to provide understanding of the proof and the tools employed.

Title/name of problem: Extended table for knotted surfaces
Short description of problem (100 words: 1-dimensional knots have been classified to great detail with a wide range of invariance properties, with repositories such as https://knotinfo.org/. The classification of Surface Knots on the other hand is complicated by various factors. There's not even a consensus on what the notion of "crossing number" should be, although there are multiple proposed definitions from different angles. Another issue we encounter is the lack of unified computational methods to encode arbitrary surface knots. One possible path is to utilize bridge trisections and triplane diagrams, although there are other diagrammatic representations of surface knots that can be encoded computationally, such as CH diagrams and banded unlink diagrams. The most recent knot table I'm aware of is Yoshikawa's table for knots in R^4 with ch-index less than 10.
Submitted Area: low dimensional topology, knotted surfaces in 4-manifolds
Reference/source material:
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2205.11120 - compiles recent results on triple point number for knots in Yoshikawa's table. 
https://projecteuclid.org/journals/osaka-journal-of-mathematics/volume-31/issue-3/An-enumeration-of-surfaces-in-four-space/ojm/1200785461.full - original source of Yoshikawa's table
Conversations with Dr. Sarah Blackwell, Dr. David Gabai and Dr. Zoltan Szabo.
Desired outcome: Figure out the "best" complexity measure for surface knots (crossing number vs ch-index vs bridge number vs others). Summarize all invariants from different mathematical tools and compile known computed invariants.

Title/name of problem: Infinite Two-Generated Groups of Bounded Exponent (Burnside Problem)
Short description of problem (100 words: Prove that there exists an infinite group G generated by two elements and satisfying the identity x^n = 1 for some positive integer n. Determine as many values of n as possible for which such a group exists. In particular, investigate the free Burnside groups B(2,n), their infinitude, and the dependence of the answer on the exponent n.
Submitted Area: Group Theory, Combinatorial Group Theory, Geometric Group Theory
Reference/source material:
S. I. Adian, The Burnside Problem and Identities in Groups. Springer, 1979. https://zbmath.org/0417.20001

A. Yu. Ol'shanskii, Geometry of Defining Relations in Groups. Kluwer, 1991. https://zbmath.org/0732.20019

A. Atkarskaya, E. Rips, K. Tent, The Burnside Problem for Odd Exponents. arXiv:2303.15997. https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.15997
Desired outcome: A rigorous proof of the existence of an infinite two-generated group of finite exponent, together with an explicit description of the construction. Participants should identify as many admissible exponents as possible, explain which cases are known, and, if feasible, improve existing bounds or develop alternative proofs.

Title/name of problem: Construction of an Infinite Finitely Presented Nilsemigroup
Short description of problem (100 words: A semigroup with zero is called a nilsemigroup if every element is nilpotent, meaning that for each element x there exists a positive integer n such that x^n = 0. Construct an infinite finitely presented nilsemigroup and prove both its infinitude and the nilpotency of all its elements. In particular, investigate constructions satisfying a uniform identity x^n = 0 and the role of finite defining relations in guaranteeing these properties.
Submitted Area: Semigroup Theory, Combinatorial Algebra, Geometric Algebra
Reference/source material:
I. A. Ivanov-Pogodaev, A. Ya. Kanel-Belov, Construction of a Nilsemigroup of Paths in a Countable Family of Uniformly Elliptic Complexes. Algebra and Logic, 63(6), 410–438 (2025). https://doi.org/10.1007/s10469-025-09803-3

I. A. Ivanov-Pogodaev, A. Ya. Kanel-Belov, Deterministic Coloring of a Family of Complexes. Fundamentalnaya i Prikladnaya Matematika, 24(2), 37–180 (2022).
Desired outcome: An explicit finite presentation of an infinite nilsemigroup, together with rigorous proofs that every element is nilpotent and that the semigroup is infinite. Participants are encouraged to explore simpler constructions, reduce the number of generators or defining relations, or establish stronger properties such as a uniform bound on nilpotency exponents.

Title/name of problem: Polynomial Identities and the Specht Problem
Short description of problem (100 words:
A polynomial identity of an associative algebra is a noncommutative polynomial that vanishes under every substitution of algebra elements.

(a) Construct an infinite system of polynomial identities that is not finitely based, working over a field of positive characteristic.

(b) Prove that, over an infinite field, if the total number of distinct variables occurring in a system of polynomial identities is bounded, then the entire system follows from a finite subsystem.

Investigate the connection with Specht's problem and T-ideals.
Submitted Area: Associative Algebra, Polynomial Identity Theory (PI-Algebras), Universal Algebra
Reference/source material:
A. Ya. Belov, Counterexamples to the Specht Problem. Sbornik: Mathematics, 191(3), 329–340 (2000). https://www.mathnet.ru/eng/sm460

A. R. Kemer, Identities of Finitely Generated Algebras over an Infinite Field. Mathematics of the USSR-Izvestiya, 37(1), 69–96 (1991). https://doi.org/10.1070/IM1991v037n01ABEH002053

Desired outcome: An explicit example of an infinitely based system of polynomial identities in an associative algebra, with a rigorous proof that no finite subsystem generates all the identities. Participants should also prove the finite basis property for systems involving a bounded number of variables under appropriate assumptions on the base field. Alternative constructions and extensions to different characteristics are welcome.

Title/name of problem: Subexponential Upper Bounds for the Nilpotency Index of Associative Algebras
Short description of problem (100 words:
Let A be an associative algebra generated by l elements and satisfying the polynomial identity x^d = 0. Its nilpotency index is the smallest integer k such that every product of k elements of A is zero.

Prove that the nilpotency index is less than Psi(d,d,l), where

Psi(n,d,l) = 2^18 · l · (nd)^(3 log_3(nd) + 13) · d^2.

Investigate possible improvements of this bound using combinatorics of words, n-divisibility, and Shirshov's height theorem.
Submitted Area: Associative Algebra, PI-Algebras, Combinatorics on Words, Ring Theory
Reference/source material:
A. Ya. Belov, M. I. Kharitonov, Subexponential Estimates in Shirshov's Theorem on Height. Sbornik: Mathematics, 203(4), 534–553 (2012). https://doi.org/10.1070/SM2012v203n04ABEH004233

A. Ya. Belov, M. I. Kharitonov, Subexponential Estimations in Shirshov's Height Theorem. arXiv:1207.2987. https://arxiv.org/abs/1207.2987

Selected Works of A. I. Shirshov. Contemporary Mathematicians, Birkhäuser, 2009.
Desired outcome: A rigorous derivation of the stated upper bound on the nilpotency index of finitely generated associative algebras satisfying x^d = 0. The primary research goal is to obtain sharper estimates, ideally improving the asymptotic dependence on d and the number of generators. Participants may develop new combinatorial arguments, refine existing techniques, or identify classes of algebras admitting substantially better bounds.

Title/name of problem: Invariant subspace problem: the Enflo–Read counterexamples
Short description of problem (100 words: The invariant subspace problem asks whether every bounded operator on a complex Banach space has a nontrivial closed invariant subspace. For general Banach spaces the answer is no. Enflo and Read constructed counterexamples, Read even on ℓ1. These constructions are long and technical and are known to few people, while the separable Hilbert space case remains open. A clearer understanding of why the counterexamples work, and what fails on Hilbert spaces, would make this classical negative result accessible.
Reference/source material:
1. C. J. Read, "A solution to the invariant subspace problem", Bull. London Math. Soc. 16 (1984), 337-401.
2. P. Enflo, "On the invariant subspace problem for Banach spaces", Acta Math. 158 (1987), 213-313.
3. C. J. Read, "A solution to the invariant subspace problem on the space l1", Bull. London Math. Soc. 17 (1985), 305-317.
Desired outcome: A clear exposition of the counterexample constructions and of what prevents them from working on Hilbert spaces.

Title/name of problem: Monsky's theorem and Stein's conjecture on equal-area dissections
Short description of problem (100 words: Monsky (1970) proved that a square cannot be cut into an odd number of equal-area triangles, via a 2-adic valuation and a Sperner-type coloring. Stein conjectured the same for centrally symmetric polygons (proved by Monsky, 1990) and for all "special" polygons, where known methods cover only rational coordinates. The proofs are short but non-constructive and unintuitive.

2. P. Monsky, "A conjecture of Stein on plane dissections", Math. Z. 205 (1990), 583-592.
3. M. Aigner, G. M. Ziegler, Proofs from THE BOOK, chapter "One square and an odd number of triangles".
Desired outcome: A valuation-light or visual proof and clarity on which special polygons known methods cover.

Title/name of problem: Non-parametric Bernstein von-Mises theorems
Short description of problem (100 words: The Bernstein von-Mises theorem states that the posterior mean centred at the ground truth is a Gaussian distribution, under suitable assumptions. Several proofs of this theorem exist in infinite dimensional settings with slightly different hypotheses. Each proof is incredibly long (50 pages) and involves many tedious optimisations of constants. The goal of this project is to unify and simplify these existing proofs in literature to provide a definitive reference BvM theorem for statisticians and formalise it in lean.
Reference/source material:
This problem was proposed jointly by my PhD supervisor Richard Nickl
[1] BvM for parabolic PDE setting https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.14781
[2]  BvM for white noise model https://projecteuclid.org/journals/annals-of-statistics/volume-42/issue-5/On-the-Bernsteinvon-Mises-phenomenon-for-nonparametric-Bayes-procedures/10.1214/14-AOS1246.full
[3] Chapter 12 in Ghosal, S. and van der Vaart, A. W. (2017). Fundamentals of Nonparametric Bayesian Inference. Cambridge University Press.
Desired outcome:
A Bernstein-von Mises theorem whose hypotheses are more general that all of the non-parametric Bernstein-von Mises theorems appearing in literature. Either a new proof that unifies these statements, or the existing proof structure with all constants optimised in each of the cases covered by the hypotheses. 
A formalisation of the above theorem +proof in lean.

Title/name of problem: A Systematic Study of Inverse Galois Problem
Short description of problem (100 words: The classification of finite simple groups was a landmark achievement in group theory. A natural next milestone is to realize every finite simple group as a Galois group over Q. A concrete way to achieve this is to construct, for each group, an explicit polynomial over Q whose splitting field has that Galois group. AI gives a promising tool to accelerate progress toward this goal.

2. The Mathieu group M23 is a Galois group over Q: https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.08538
Desired outcome: A systematic understanding of solved inverse Galois problems and exploring more unknown cases.

Title/name of problem: Monochromatic Triangles in the Plane
Short description of problem (100 words:
The problem was to determine whether there is a universal constant C such that, for any n points in convex position, at most C*n pairs of points can be exactly distance 1 apart.

This problem has now been solved: no such constant exists.
Reference/source material:
The proof exposition is found in the following paper:
Unit distances in convex polygons - Liam Kruer, Jensen Kohlmeyer, and Liam Price - https://liamkruer.com/assets/work/erdos-96-97/96-97.pdf
Desired outcome:
Something that interested me from the Mathathon homepage was the suggestion to explain a proof via "an interactive game", as that seemed like a good challenge. It is also something that seems very possible now with coding help from AI. The construction in the cited paper my best candidate for an incredible recent result that could possibly be turned into a game. 

Therefore, the creation I would like to see participants create is a playable proof. The basic goal of the game would be to guide a player towards inventing/discovering the ideas for the construction, so that they understand the full proof well afterwards.

The successful use of the medium of games may still be difficult, and it may be that the end result is more of an interactive read-through of the steps in the proof, with visuals. But for this project, I want us to explore how to use gameplay to make the understanding of this proof more accessible or efficient. Ideally, game mechanics will add to the experience.

I would prefer/recommend using Godot game engine for building the application.

Title/name of problem: Existence of the Core in Approval-Based Committee Elections

Title/name of problem: Lagrange Inversion: Combinatorial Proofs
