Title/name of problem: The Cap Set Problem and the Slice Rank Method
Short description of problem (100 words: In 2016, Ellenberg and Gijswijt, building on Croot-Lev-Pach, proved that a cap set in F_3^n has size O(2.756^n). The proof is strikingly short, using polynomials and what Tao later named the “slice rank” of a function. Yet it remains unclear why this approach succeeds where Fourier methods stalled, how robust it is, and which other patterns, fields, and geometric or colouring problems it can reach.
Submitted Area: Additive combinatorics, algebraic combinatorics, polynomial method
Reference/source material:
J. S. Ellenberg and D. Gijswijt, “On large subsets of F_q^n with no three-term arithmetic progression,” Annals of Mathematics 185 (2017), 339-343.
E. Croot, V. Lev, and P. P. Pach, “Progression-free sets in Z_4^n are exponentially small,” Annals of Mathematics 185 (2017), 331-337.
E. Naslund, “Monochromatic equilateral triangles in the unit distance graph,” Bulletin of the London Mathematical Society 52 (2020).
Desired outcome:
We would like teams to build a clear, verifiable understanding of the slice rank method, starting from its cap set origins and then testing how far it extends. Possible deliverables include a formalization (for example in Lean) of the slice rank lemma and the Ellenberg-Gijswijt bound, an exposition or interactive tool for visualizing slice rank on small examples, or an analysis of which assumptions in the method are essential and which can be relaxed. Teams could also explore how the technique carries over to related avoidance problems, including settings where the functions are not strictly polynomial or the forbidden configuration is geometric rather than purely additive. 

The topic has a short, accessible core proof and a lot of room around it. Teams can start from pure formalization or exposition and, if time allows, push toward new applications. Several adjacent results (e.g., Naslund’s geometric application) show the method’s reach beyond the original setting, so there is room for original work as well as consolidation.

Title/name of problem: Stanley's poset inequality
Short description of problem (100 words: Let $N_k$ count the linear extensions of a poset that place a given element $a$ at position $k$. Stanley proved $N_k^2\ge N_{k-1}N_{k+1}$ by applying Alexandrov–Fenchel to order polytopes, and Kahn and Saks used this for a sorting theorem. A discrete count thus rests on deep convex geometry. Chan and Pak give a linear-algebraic proof.
Submitted Area: Combinatorics; convex geometry; toric geometry; algorithms
Reference/source material: (1) R. Stanley, Two combinatorial applications of the Aleksandrov–Fenchel inequalities, J. Combin. Theory Ser. A 31 (1981), 56–65. (2) J. Kahn, M. Saks, Balancing poset extensions, Order 1 (1984), 113–126. (3) S. H. Chan, I. Pak, Log-concave poset inequalities, arXiv:2110.10740.
Desired outcome: A proof of the inequality using toric geometry, in which mixed volumes become intersection numbers, compared against the Chan-Pak proof. Alternatively, find a purely combinatoric proof.

Title/name of problem: The circulant Hadamard conjecture
Short description of problem (100 words: A real circulant Hadamard matrix has order 1 or 4, which also classifies Barker sequences. This problem about $\pm1$ sequences resisted decades of work. The new 15-page proof reduces to $n=4u^2$, then shows an alternating product of character values is an algebraic integer whose conjugates all have absolute value 1. Kronecker's theorem and analysis finish.
Reference/source material: (1) OpenAI, The circulant Hadamard conjecture (23 September 2026), https://github.com/openai/math/tree/main/preprints/The-circulant-Hadamard-conjecture-September-23-2026 (2) R. Turyn, Character sums and difference sets, Pacific J. Math. 15 (1965), 319–346. (3) B. Schmidt, Cyclotomic integers and finite geometry, J. AMS 12 (1999), 929–952.
Desired outcome: An explanation of where the "black magic" alternating product comes from and how it relates to earlier field-descent methods.

Title/name of problem: Topological Drinfeld homomorphism and the strong Macdonald conjecture
Short description of problem (100 words: For a simply connected space X and a complex reductive algebraic group G, the Drinfeld homomorphism maps a free graded-commutative algebra on selected Hodge components of circle-equivariant free-loop homology of X to G-invariant representation homology of X. Both sides have topological interpretations. Berest, Ramadoss, and Yeung prove this map is an isomorphism for specified spaces using Fishel, Grojnowski, and Teleman’s cohomology results for truncated current Lie algebras and a related Lie superalgebra-the two cases of the strong Macdonald conjecture. The challenge is to prove the isomorphism topologically without those results, or construct the trace directly from topology.
Submitted Area: Algebraic topology, rational homotopy theory, representation theory, and Lie algebra cohomology
Reference/source material:
1. Yuri Berest, Ajay C. Ramadoss, and Wai-Kit Yeung, “Representation homology of simply connected spaces”, Journal of Topology 15 (2022), 692-744.

2. Susanna Fishel, Ian Grojnowski, and Constantin Teleman, “The strong Macdonald conjecture and Hodge theory on the loop Grassmannian”, Annals of Mathematics 168 (2008), 175-220.

3. Yuri Berest, Giovanni Felder, Sasha Patotski, Ajay C. Ramadoss, and Thomas Willwacher, “Representation homology, Lie algebra cohomology and the derived Harish-Chandra homomorphism”, Journal of the European Mathematical Society 19 (2017), 2811-2893.
Desired outcome: A direct topological construction of the Drinfeld homomorphism that agrees with the existing map, or a topological proof that the Drinfeld homomorphism is an isomorphism for the specified spaces without using Fishel-Grojnowski-Teleman’s cohomology results. A full proof, translated through the known comparisons with Lie algebra cohomology, would provide an independent topological proof of both cases of the strong Macdonald conjecture. Fishel, Grojnowski, and Teleman originally proved it in full generality through a demanding algebraic argument.

Title/name of problem: Understanding Matrix Multiplication
Short description of problem (100 words: Recent constructions achieve a matrix multiplication exponent approaching 9/4, yet their asymptotic operation counts conceal enormous finite costs. A starting point could be from the polynomial packing construction in Rafael Pass's paper, by investigating how its algebraic savings become a recursive algorithm. There are several things to consider, like polynomial packing, interpolation, approximate identities conversion, etc.
Submitted Area: Algebraic Complexity Theory, Numerical Linear Algebra
Reference/source material:
1. https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.28627 by Rafael Pass. Primary reference for the construction and its conversion into an explicit recursive algorithm.
2. https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0603207v3 by James Demmel, Ioana Dumitriu, Olga Holtz, and Robert Kleinberg. Reference for the relationship between fast multiplication and numerical stability.
Desired outcome:
An exposition of an existing fast matrix multiplication construction.
- Small, exact worked examples that reveal the construction's key ideas.
- Reproducible symbolic computations and visualizations.
- An explicit analysis of how block dimensions, coefficient sizes, and operation counts depend on the chosen exponent, clarifying the gap between asymptotic efficiency and practical computation.

Potentially a connection to numerical analysis that clarifies precision requirements too. Although the reference construction already includes an asymptotic bit-complexity analysis.

Title/name of problem: The Painlevé paradox
Short description of problem (100 words: A rigid rod moving on a rough surface can reach conditions where the equations predict either multiple motions or no valid motion. Explain how this occurs under Coulomb friction. Then explain how a compliant contact model changes the result. Develop a clear account of one published result, with diagrams that show the relevant parameter regimes and the assumptions behind the proof.
Reference/source material: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5493941/
Desired outcome: A visual explanation and a worked proof for a restricted case. A small simulation would support the explanation.

Title/name of problem: Surface intersection with correct topology
Short description of problem (100 words: Two curved CAD surfaces can intersect in several disconnected curves, including small closed loops. Explain a published method that preserves the topology of the intersection while controlling approximation error. Identify the assumptions needed for its guarantee. Use simple surface families to show how tangency and singular points complicate the problem, and why a small geometric error alone does not establish correct connectivity.
Submitted Area: Computational geometry, algebraic geometry, numerical analysis
Reference/source material: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0167839625000214?via%3Dihub
Desired outcome: An accessible explanation of the guarantee, an illustrated restricted case, and examples that expose the method’s limits.

Title/name of problem: Chowla’s conjecture for two-point correlations
Short description of problem (100 words: Let \lambda(n)=(-1)^{Omega(n)}, where \Omega(n) counts prime factors with multiplicity. The estimate \sum_{n\le x}\lambda(n)=o(x) is equivalent to the famous prime number theorem. The two-point Chowla conjecture asserts that \sum_{n\le x}\lambda(n)\lambda(n+h)=o(x) for every fixed positive integer h. So the parities of the numbers of prime factors of n and n+h are asymptotically uncorrelated. These type of question, while still very difficults, serve as a simpler model for questions about correlations of primes, including the twin prime conjecture. OpenAI recently announced a proof.
Reference/source material:
OpenAI manuscript with claimed solution
https://github.com/openai/math/blob/main/preprints/Ordinary-two-point-correlations-of-multiplicative-functions-September-24-2026/final.pdf

Averaged variant of the conjecture was proved by Matomaki-Radziwiłł-Tao
"An averaged form of Chowla's conjecture." Algebra Number Theory 9 (2015) DOI: 10.2140/ant.2015.9.2167

Best known bound for the logarithmic variant of the conjecture:
Cédric Pilatte. "Improved bounds for the two-point logarithmic Chowla conjecture." Journal of the American Mathematical Society DOI: 10.1090/jams/1084
Desired outcome:
I would like there to be survey  explaining: outline of the proof, key ideas, new techniques and their comparison to previous works and maybe other areas of mathematics.
The goal would be to understand how agument developed instead of just seeing a sequence of true claims and share it with others in a survey note.
Another goal (but less reliable) could be to attempt (with AI assistance) to simplify the proof.

Title/name of problem: Cannon's conjecture and friends
Short description of problem (100 words: Cannon's conjecture, which OpenAI has apparently proven, states that any hyperbolic group with Gromov boundary homeomorphic to a 2-sphere is virtually isomorphic to a cocompact Kleinian group. The convergence group theorem of Gabai gives an analogous result for hyperbolic groups with boundary homeomorphic to the circle. In broad strokes, these can be regarded as rigidity results for group actions on low-dimensional spheres. Could we produce a more conceptual, digestible proof of Cannon's conjecture, and are there any unifying threads between the proofs of these and other related results?
Reference/source material:
1. OpenAI write-up @ https://github.com/openai/math/tree/main/preprints/A-Modulus-Proof-of-Cannons-Conjecture-September-23-2026 
2. David Gabai, "Convergence groups are Fuchsian groups" @ https://www.projecteuclid.org/journalArticle/Download?urlid=bams%2F1183657188
3. G. Christopher Hruska and Genevieve Walsh, "Relatively hyperbolic groups with planar boundaries" @ https://arxiv.org/html/2405.20428v1 re: some related statements and extensions
Desired outcome: An expository write-up and/or video

Title/name of problem: Exotic hyperbolic groups from 2-complexes
Short description of problem (100 words: Recent results of OpenAI, and subsequent follow-ups, have claimed a number of word-hyperbolic groups with "exotic" properties: (1) a word-hyperbolic group which is not residually finite; (2) a word-hyperbolic group which does not act geometrically on any CAT(0) space; (3) a non-sofic word-hyperbolic group. All three examples appear to involve the construction of certain 2-dimensional complexes, starting with suitable incidence graphs. How similar are these constructions, or is it simply an sufficiently flexible general construction?
Reference/source material:
1. OpenAI non-RF group @ https://github.com/openai/math/blob/main/preprints/a-torsion-free-hyperbolic-group-that-is-not-residually-finite-September-23-2026/paper.pdf
2. OpenAI non-CAT(0) group @ https://github.com/openai/math/blob/main/preprints/A-hyperbolic-group-with-no-geometric-CAT0-action-September-25-2026/paper.pdf
3. H. Sandhu and A. Thom, "An example of a non-sofic hyperbolic group" @ https://arxiv.org/html/2610.24836
Desired outcome: An expository write-up; code to generate and visualize(?) 2-complexes from the construction

Title/name of problem: Different Effective Equation with shared Brownian Limit
Short description of problem (100 words: Two microscopic random walks can converge to Brownian motions with identical covariance while producing different limiting equations when used as driving signals. Their iterated integrals retain an area correction invisible to ordinary path convergence. So a contribution could be a complete reproducible passage from transition probabilities to the effective equation (reconstructing it for a finite-state Markov model and its time reversal).
Submitted Area: Probability, Stochastic Differential Equations, and Dynamical Systems.
Reference/source material:
1. https://arxiv.org/abs/1709.04288 by Olga Lopusanschi and Damien Simon. Sections 1 and 2 establish enhanced convergence and identify the area correction.
2. https://doi.org/10.3934/cpaa.2026046 by Maximilian Engel, Peter Friz, Tal Orenshtein. They have a nice discrete-time discussion.
3. https://www.hairer.org/notes/RoughPaths.pdf by Peter Friz and Martin Hairer. Chapter 8 treats Ito-Lyons map's continuity and explains how enhanced driving signals determine solution limits.
Desired outcome: A worked proof and reproducible demonstration showing exactly where microscopic temporal asymmetry survives the limit. For example, use a stationary 3-state Markov chain with simple designed increments, and compare it with its time reversal. Or on piecewise-linear walks, calculate the limiting covariance and antisymmetric area correction exactly.

Title/name of problem: Ulam Floating Problem perimetral density 1/3,1/4,1/5
Short description of problem (100 words: The Ulam Floating Problem, first proposed by the Scottish book, has been solved in perimetral density (the waterline cuts the arclength into equal pieces) for 1/2,1/3,1/4,1/5,1/6,1/7,1/8, and, although the proofs haven't been released yet, the 1/10 case. For 1/2, it can be a shape other than a disk, but for 1/n where n>2, it has been proven to be rigid (a disk). There is a current bottleneck in how these are proven; the proofs rely on symmetries and don't generalize well to larger n based on the limitations of symmetries.
Reference/source material:
https://arxiv.org/html/2607.08338v1#bib.bib8 1/8 & 3/8 cases
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2604.10330 1/6 case
https://matwbn.icm.edu.pl/ksiazki/sm/sm7/sm7112.pdf 1/2 case
Desired outcome: I would like to see a new framework for solving this problem that is less constrained by symmetries and can generalize to larger n values. If possible, I would like to see some useful math strategies come out of this, just as solving this problem helped develop the Zindler Carousel formulation which has been useful in the past, maybe this can happen again.

Title/name of problem: Towards a uniform natural proof of the nonnesting-noncrossing correspondence, starting with type B
Short description of problem (100 words: For every Weyl group W and Coxeter element c, nonnesting and noncrossing partitions are known to be equal in number, counted by Cat(W) = prod_i (h+d_i)/d_i, with matching cyclic actions. The existing proof is unsatisfying. Armstrong-Stump-Thomas give an equivariant bijection, but in their own words "the proof that our construction is well-defined is case-by-case, using a computer in the exceptional types", and it covers only bipartite c. Dequêne et al. (2022) call the relationship "frustratingly mysterious" and give a natural proof via charmed roots in type A (type C follows by folding). Type B, where folding fails, still has none.
Reference/source material:
1. D. Armstrong, C. Stump, H. Thomas, "A uniform bijection between nonnesting and noncrossing partitions", Trans. Amer. Math. Soc. (2013), arXiv:1101.1277 (Main Theorem; case-by-case proof in Section 5).
2. C. Dequêne, G. Frieden, A. Iraci, F. Schreier-Aigner, H. Thomas, N. Williams, "Charmed roots and the Kroweras complement", arXiv:2212.14831 (Problem 1.3; type A bijection in Section 5; type C by folding and the proposed uniform extension in Section 7).
Desired outcome: The ideal goal is a proof of the nonnesting-noncrossing correspondence that explains it uniformly, instead of checking it type by type. Dequêne et al. propose a uniform definition of charmed roots for all Weyl groups, but it has only been made to work in type A (and type C by folding). Type B is the natural first test: does the proposed definition give local rules for an equivariant, support-preserving bijection there, for every Coxeter element, and if not, what has to change? Minimum: explicit computations for B_3, B_4 and an account of where the type A rules break. Target: rules verified by computer for all c up to B_5. Stretch: a proof for all n in type B, and a clear picture of what a uniform construction would need. Maybe also a visual exposition of the bijection in small cases.

Title/name of problem: Classification of minimal cones.
Short description of problem (100 words: A possible project is to extend Taylor’s classification of singularities for minimizing surfaces from R3 to Rn, beginning with R4. A second direction is to study anisotropic energies, where the angles between the planes need not be the same.
Reference/source material: (https://www.jstor.org/stable/1970950 ) The Structure of Singularities in Solutions to Ellipsoidal Variational Problems With Constraints in R3 by Jean Taylor, Vol. 103, No. 3 (May, 1976).
Desired outcome: Hopefully, we could classify the minimizing cones in Rn. I suspect that there will be n+1 many cones. Additionally, I am interested to know the other minimal candidates.

Title/name of problem: Projectivity of Gieseker Moduli on the Projective Plane without GIT
Short description of problem (100 words: Good moduli spaces offer a way to revisit classical moduli constructions without relying on geometric invariant theory (GIT) quotients. Following the blueprint of Alper and collaborators for vector bundles on curves, we aim to give a proof of projectivity for the moduli space of Gieseker-semistable torsion-free sheaves on the projective plane with arbitrary fixed rank and Chern classes. We will use AHLH '23 to obtain a proper good moduli space, construct a finite morphism to a Kronecker quiver moduli space, and prove projectivity by pulling back its ample determinantal line bundle.
Reference/source material:
Jarod Alper, Daniel Halpern-Leistner, and Jochen Heinloth, “Existence of moduli spaces for algebraic stacks,” Inventiones Mathematicae 234 (2023)

Luis Álvarez-Cónsul and Alastair King, “A functorial construction of moduli of sheaves,” Inventiones Mathematicae 168 (2007), 613–666.

Pieter Belmans, Chiara Damiolini, Hans Franzen, Victoria Hoskins, Svetlana Makarova, and Tuomas Tajakka, “Projectivity and effective global generation of determinantal line bundles on quiver moduli,” Algebra & Number Theory 20 (2026), no. 4.
Desired outcome: A short expository note giving a proof of projectivity for the moduli space of Gieseker-semistable torsion-free sheaves on the projective plane with arbitrary fixed rank and Chern classes, without using classical GIT quotients.

Title/name of problem: Gittins Index Optimality for Scheduling with Time-Varying Holding Costs
Short description of problem (100 words:
How should we schedule jobs when the cost of delaying them increases over time? Consider a single server processing two classes of randomly arriving jobs. Each class has an increasing holding-cost function (c_i(t)), specifying the cost incurred per unit time by a job that has waited (t) time units since arrival. Our goal is to minimize the total expected cost of delay (see Li et al., 2026, §3.1).

This problem belongs to a notoriously difficult class of stochastic optimization problems called restless multi-armed bandits. We have developed a conditional result establishing the optimality of a Gittins-index scheduling policy. Can its proof be simplified or generalized?
Submitted Area: Applied probability, stochastic optimization, Markov decision processes, queueing theory, multi-armed bandits.
Reference/source material:
Gurushankar, K. Threshold MDP and Index POMDP. Unpublished manuscript. Theorem 1.7 states the conditional Gittins-index optimality result, with the mathematical argument developed in Sections 2–3 and Appendix A. Available from the proposer.

Li, Z., Gurushankar, K., Harchol-Balter, M., and Scheller-Wolf, A. (2026). Improving Upon the Generalized cμ Rule: A Whittle Approach. Operations Research. https://doi.org/10.1287/opre.2025.1987
Sections 3.1–3.2 formally define the scheduling problem and its equivalent restless multi-armed bandit formulation.

Gurushankar, K., Li, Z., Harchol-Balter, M., and Scheller-Wolf, A. (2026). LookAhead: The Optimal Non-decreasing Index Policy for a Time-Varying Holding Cost Problem. Queueing Systems, 110, Article 7. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11134-025-09967-w
Establishes index optimality for a special case in which one job class has constant holding costs.
Desired outcome:
A simpler or more intuitive proof of the conditional Gittins-index optimality result, or a rigorous verification of its key arguments.

In classical multi-armed bandits, the Gittins index provides a remarkably simple optimal strategy: assign each option a priority based only on its own state and always choose the highest-priority option. This elegant result generally fails for restless bandits, where the states of unselected options continue to evolve.

Our scheduling problem has exactly this difficulty: a job becomes more costly to delay even when another job is being served.

The existing conditional proof uses several mathematical ideas, including Markov decision processes with age thresholds, consistency of optimal policies under different thresholds, and a construction that assigns priorities by considering the cost of serving versus waiting.

We would welcome alternative proofs that make these connections clearer, identify which assumptions are essential, or extend parts of the argument to other restless bandit problems.

Participants could focus on a particular lemma or proof technique rather than reproducing the entire result.

Title/name of problem: A classification of finite Euclidean Ramsey configurations
Short description of problem (100 words: A finite set X ⊂ ℝⁿ is Ramsey if for every r, every r-colouring of ℝᵐ (m large) contains a monochromatic congruent copy of X. Erdős et al. (1973) showed Ramsey sets are spherical. Graham conjectured the converse, and Leader, Russell and Walters (2012) conjectured that Ramsey sets are exactly the subtransitive ones. OpenAI's publication claims a complete classification via a tensor condition over the coordinate fields. It follows that every subtransitive set and every set of at most five concyclic points is Ramsey, and that some Ramsey cyclic quadrilaterals are not subtransitive.
Reference/source material:
OpenAI, “A classification of finite Euclidean Ramsey configurations”, preprint, 23 September 2026. https://github.com/openai/math/tree/main/preprints/A-classification-of-finite-Euclidean-Ramsey-configurations-September-23-2026 (Lean formalisation: lean/docs/172.md in the same repository, uses "sorry" everywhere)
P. Erdős, R. L. Graham, P. Montgomery, B. L. Rothschild, J. Spencer, E. G. Straus, “Euclidean Ramsey theorems I”, J. Combin. Theory Ser. A 14 (1973), 341–363.
I. Leader, P. A. Russell, M. Walters, “Transitive sets in Euclidean Ramsey theory”, J. Combin. Theory Ser. A 119 (2012), 382–396.
Desired outcome:
- Independent human verification of the tensor criterion, with an explanation of its geometric meaning.
- A readable, self-contained proof of a special case, e.g. that every cyclic quadrilateral is Ramsey.
- An explicit check of the counterexample: a concrete Ramsey cyclic quadrilateral that is not subtransitive, with a proof that it is not.
- Maybe Lean formalization?

Title/name of problem: Erdős Problem #173: monochromatic congruent triangles in 2-colourings of the plane

The conjectured exception is an equilateral triangle. In October 2026, Plasma AI released a claimed proof found by GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5

Title/name of problem: An improvement towards bounded gaps between primes
Short description of problem (100 words: Zhang (2013) proved that some prime gap occurs infinitely often. Later refinements brought the bound down: Maynard's multidimensional Selberg sieve gave H₁ ≤ 600, and Polymath 8b refined it to H₁ ≤ 246. That bound stood for more than a decade, then fell several times within days in 2026. Stadlmann proved 240 using an admissible 49-tuple, Axiom built on her work to reach 212, and OpenAI's "Improved Short Gaps Between Primes" proves DHL[40,2], giving 186, and attributes the proof to GPT-6 Astra.
Reference/source material: OpenAI, Improved Short Gaps Between Primes (Aug 2026), plus the GitHub repo openai/PrimeGaps186 (Lean 4 proof and Python-FLINT certificate)
Desired outcome: How the GPY and Maynard–Tao methods turn "two primes in a translate" into an optimization over sieve weights.

Title/name of problem: Summing multiplicative functions/counting primes
Short description of problem (100 words: Fast algorithms to compute the cumulative sum of a multiplicative function and to count the number of primes less than or equal to a given n
Reference/source material: https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.09857

Title/name of problem: Quasi-Orders For the Lefthanded Lovász Local Lemma
Short description of problem (100 words:
Problem: Explain how qausi-order in the Lefthanded Lovász Local Lemma 

Description: The Lovász Local Lemma (LLL) is a theorem in the probabilistic method for proving the existence of objects satisfying properties which are sufficiently likely and sufficiently independent. Pegden introduced a lefthanded version (LLLL) of the LLL which allows the the notion of independence to be directed --- dependence on events "to the left" do not count.  

All known concrete applications of LLLL use a linear order to specify what "to the left" means. However, the theorem statement allows a quasi-order with a certain, somewhat opaque property. It would be nice to have a better understanding of what this property is and  what it buys us.
Reference/source material: Wesley Pegden. 2011. Highly nonrepetitive sequences: Winning strategies from the local lemma. Random Struct. Algorithms 38, 1–2 (January 2011), 140–161. https://doi.org/10.1002/rsa.20354  https://arxiv.org/pdf/1010.5772
Desired outcome: Any exposition of the quasi-order would be good. An application for which the quasi-order is not a linear order and an explanation of why the quasi-order helps would be very nice

Title/name of problem: Counterexamples to polynomial removal for ordered binary matrices
Short description of problem (100 words:
In a manuscript released on October 6, 2026, OpenAI showed that polynomial removal fails for ordered binary matrices, answering a question of Alon, Fischer, and Newman (2007). They had proven that in the unordered case (both rows and columns can be permuted), the answer is yes. Alon and Ben-Eliezer (2020) showed that if you allow only row permutations, the answer is still yes.

OpenAI's counterexample is a 66x66 binary matrix. Five days later, Wang used similar methods to produce a 4x4 one.

Both proofs construct complicated host matrices, which we think could be better explained and simplified.
Reference/source material:
1. Noga Alon, Eldar Fischer and Ilan Newman, "Efficient Testing of Bipartite Graphs for Forbidden Induced Subgraphs", SIAM J. Comput. 37(3) (2007), 959–976. https://doi.org/10.1137/050627915
2. OpenAI, "Polynomial removal fails for ordered binary matrices", OpenAI Math Release preprint, dated September 25, 2026, released October 6, 2026, Theorem 1.1. https://github.com/openai/math/blob/main/preprints/Polynomial-removal-fails-for-ordered-binary-matrices-September-25-2026/paper.pdf
3. Zinan Wang, "A Four-by-Four Obstruction to Polynomial Removal for Ordered Binary Matrices", arXiv:2610.15370, October 11, 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.15370
Desired outcome:
A short, human-readable proof that Wang's 4x4 matrix is a counterexample, with pictures of the first few host matrices. Connections to similar problems, for example, removal lemmas for ordered graphs or for permutation patterns, whose occurrences are ordered copies of permutation matrices.

Both counterexamples come with Lean formalizations, so what is missing is understanding, not correctness.

Title/name of problem: Model Completeness of the Real Exponential Field
Short description of problem (100 words: Consider the ordered real exponential field \(\mathbb{R}_{\exp}=(\mathbb{R};0,1,+,-,\cdot,<,\exp)\). The problem is to establish whether its complete first-order theory is model complete; that is, whether every embedding between models of this theory is elementary. Equivalently, can every first-order formula be expressed as an existential formula? Alex Wilkie proved this in 1996 using techniques involving restricted Pfaffian functions, quasipolynomial equations, o-minimality, and valuation theory. A central challenge is transferring solutions of exponential-polynomial equations between non-Archimedean models, particularly when solutions are unbounded.
Submitted Area: Mathematical Logic — Model Theory, O-minimality, Real Algebraic Geometry, and Exponential Fields.
Reference/source material:
1. A. J. Wilkie, *Model completeness results for expansions of the ordered field of real numbers by restricted Pfaffian functions and the exponential function*, Journal of the American Mathematical Society **9** (1996), no. 4, 1051–1094. https://doi.org/10.1090/S0894-0347-96-00216-0

3. A. J. Wilkie, *On the Theory of the Real Exponential Field*, Illinois Journal of Mathematics **33** (1989), no. 3, 384–408.
Desired outcome:
The primary goal is to explore alternative approaches to proving the model completeness of the real exponential field, potentially using techniques from model theory, o-minimality, real algebraic geometry, or valuation theory. Participants are encouraged to investigate whether Wilkie's original proof can be simplified or reconstructed using different mathematical methods. A further objective is to formalize the theorem and its supporting results in Lean, contributing toward a machine-verified proof. Ideally, the project would produce a detailed mathematical exposition of an alternative proof strategy alongside a Lean formalization of the established results.

This is an established but technically challenging theorem, making it suitable for exploring mathematical proof techniques and formal verification. A complete alternative proof or Lean formalization may be ambitious, so partial results, formalization of intermediate lemmas, and identification of the main obstacles would also be valuable contributions. Participants are welcome to approach the problem from either a theoretical or a formalization-oriented perspective.

Title/name of problem: An Elementary Proof of the Deligne–Sullivan Theorem and Virtual Stable Parallelizability of Compact Hyperbolic Manifolds
Short description of problem (100 words: A theorem of Sullivan, building on joint work with Deligne, establishes that every compact hyperbolic manifold is virtually stably parallelizable; that is, some finite-sheeted cover has a stably trivial tangent bundle. Existing proofs rely on sophisticated techniques from algebraic geometry, étale homotopy theory, and arithmetic topology. The problem is to find a more elementary and accessible proof of this result, ideally avoiding the Deligne–Sullivan theorem, or alternatively to develop a simpler proof of the Deligne–Sullivan theorem itself. The challenge is to replace the technically demanding arguments with more direct geometric, topological, or algebraic methods.
Submitted Area: Differential Geometry, Algebraic Topology, Geometric Topology, Hyperbolic Geometry, and Algebraic Geometry.
Reference/source material:
1. D. Sullivan, *Hyperbolic Geometry and Homeomorphisms*, in Geometric Topology, Academic Press (1979), pp. 543–555. Particularly the section "Hyperbolic space forms," pp. 9–10 of the original manuscript.
https://repo-archives.ihes.fr/FONDS_IHES/I_Prepublications/SULLIVAN/1974-1995/M_78_200B/M_78_200B.pdf

2. P. Deligne and D. Sullivan, *Fibrés vectoriels complexes à groupe structural discret*, Comptes Rendus de l'Académie des Sciences de Paris, Série A, Vol. 281 (1975), pp. 1081–1083.
https://publications.ias.edu/sites/default/files/28_FibresVectoriels.pdf

3. D. Sullivan, *Genetics of Homotopy Theory and the Adams Conjecture*, Annals of Mathematics, Vol. 100, No. 1 (1974), pp. 1–79. Particularly Theorem 3.1 concerning the Hasse principle for maps.
https://doi.org/10.2307/1970841
Desired outcome: The primary goal is to develop a simpler, more accessible proof that every compact hyperbolic manifold is virtually stably parallelizable, preferably without relying on the technically demanding Deligne–Sullivan theorem. Alternatively, one could investigate a more elementary proof of the Deligne–Sullivan theorem itself.

Title/name of problem: Towards a combinatorial proof of Schur positivity for LLT polynomials of unit interval graphs
Short description of problem (100 words: LLT polynomials of unit interval graphs are known to be Schur positive: every Schur coefficient is a polynomial in q with nonnegative integer coefficients. The existing proofs are unsatisfying: Grojnowski-Haiman express the coefficients through Kazhdan-Lusztig theory of affine Hecke algebras, and Guay-Paquet's second proof uses Hessenberg varieties, which, as Alexandersson-Sulzgruber put it, gives positivity "but no combinatorial formula for the coefficients". Combinatorial rules are known only for special families (e.g. Roberts for maximum area at most 2, Huh-Nam-Yoo for melting lollipops), and none is known for unit interval graphs in general.
Reference/source material:
1. I. Grojnowski, M. Haiman, "Affine Hecke algebras and positivity of LLT and Macdonald polynomials", preprint (2007), available at math.berkeley.edu/~mhaiman.
2. M. Guay-Paquet, "A second proof of the Shareshian-Wachs conjecture, by way of a new Hopf algebra" (2016), arXiv:1601.05498 (Schur positivity of unit interval graph LLT polynomials follows from this, as noted by Alexandersson-Sulzgruber, arXiv:2004.09198).
3. A. Roberts, "Dual equivalence graphs revisited and the explicit Schur expansion of a family of LLT polynomials", J. Algebraic Combin. (2014), arXiv:1302.0319 (Theorem 4.3).
Desired outcome:
A combinatorial proof of Schur positivity for every unit interval graph would be nice: an explicit description of what each Schur coefficient counts, together with a reason why it works.

Fortunately we do already have natural starting points; combinatorial rules already exist for some families: Roberts' rule covers every graph without a K_4, and Huh-Nam-Yoo's covers melting lollipops. But each rule already breaks on a 4-vertex graph where the other works (K_4, and a triangle with a tail). So perhaps a first goal is to understand these failures and find one rule that handles both.

And even if the full problem is too much for the mathathon, we can start with a natural test case: K-chains (chains of cliques glued at single vertices), which are the simplest graphs containing a K_4 that no known rule covers. The interesting ones contain a K_4 with something attached on both sides (Roberts' rule fails on 11 of the 14 such graphs with 8 vertices, for example). Thus, we could start with establishing a rule that is correct on all K-chains with 8 vertices, and work towards a proof for the whole family.

Title/name of problem: Hironaka’s Resolution of Singularity: Understanding the Algorithm and Its Later Simplifications
Short description of problem (100 words: Hironaka’s theorem states that every algebraic variety over a field of characteristic zero admits a resolution of singularities. Develop an accessible explanation of how a modern resolution algorithm chooses blowup centers, measures progress, and guarantees termination. Use nontrivial worked examples to explain why naive choices can fail, and compare how later approaches, particularly those of Bierstone–Milman and Włodarczyk, clarified the construction and simplified its proof. The goal is to connect explicit local calculations with the logic of the general theorem.
Reference/source material:
Herwig Hauser, “The Hironaka theorem on resolution of singularities (or: A proof we always wanted to understand),” Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society 40 (2003).

Edward Bierstone and Pierre D. Milman, “Resolution of Singularities,” Several Complex Variables, MSRI Publications 37 (1999).

Jarosław Włodarczyk, “Simple Hironaka resolution in characteristic zero,” Journal of the American Mathematical Society 18 (2005).
Desired outcome:
A rigorous, accessible exposition of a modern proof of Hironaka’s theorem, supported by worked examples and, where useful, interactive visualizations or symbolic computation. The project should include:
- A complete walkthrough of a nontrivial surface example, explaining the chosen centers, coordinate charts, exceptional components, and measures of progress.
- A contrasting example showing why a plausible but naive sequence of blowups fails.
- An explanation of the mechanism guaranteeing termination and how local constructions fit together.
- A focused comparison of later improvements, distinguishing more systematic constructions, compatibility with coordinate changes, and simplifications of the proof.

Title/name of problem: Unraveling Preiss' Geometry of Measures

We propose an interactive exposition combining a multiscale proof graph with geometric laboratories. Working through selected arguments, AI agents and human reviewers will reconstruct dependencies, clarify hypotheses, and develop alternative explanations. Initial modules will investigate tangent measures, the Kowalski–Preiss cone, and the passage from one flat tangent to flatness of all tangents under the appropriate hypotheses. The aim is to make the proof’s mechanisms explorable, while preserving precise statements, source attribution, and a transparent record of AI contributions.
Reference/source material:
David Preiss, “Geometry of measures in (\mathbb R^n): Distribution, rectifiability, and densities,” Annals of Mathematics 125 (1987), 537–643. 

Camillo De Lellis, Rectifiable Sets, Densities, and Tangent Measures, Zürich Lectures in Advanced Mathematics, EMS, 2008
Desired outcome: A carefully checked, interactive exposition that helps readers explain why the obvious proof fails and how Preiss repairs it. The initial deliverable will combine an overview graph, a detailed treatment of one central argument, and geometric demonstrations built from matlab (or other software). A reproducible repository will contain code, original explanatory material, source references, and relevant AI records. The two-month continuation will expand and refine the exposition. Alternative proofs or simplifications will also be sought.

Title/name of problem: Why regular polygons have the fewest distances: an illustrated guide to Altman's theorem
Short description of problem (100 words: Erdős conjectured, and Altman proved in 1963, that the vertices of a convex n-gon determine at least ⌊n/2⌋ distinct distances; for odd n, only the regular n-gon has exactly that many. For even n ≥ 8, Fishburn showed in 1995 that the extremal polygons are the regular n-gon and the regular (n+1)-gon minus a vertex. The proofs use only elementary geometry but are dense with indices and cases, so few people know why the answers are what they are. The barrier to entry is low: everything needs only high-school geometry.
Submitted Area: Discrete geometry (Euclidean plane geometry and extremal combinatorics)
Reference/source material:
1. E. Altman, "On a problem of P. Erdős", Amer. Math. Monthly 70 (1963) 148–157, doi:10.2307/2312883. The Theorem (p. 149), proved with Lemmas 1 and 2 (pp. 149–153); the theorem on regular (2N+1)-gons and Lemma 3 (pp. 153–157).
2. E. Altman, "Some theorems on convex polygons", Canad. Math. Bull. 15 (1972) 329–340, doi:10.4153/CMB-1972-060-0. A second proof of the bound: §III, Lemma 1 and Theorem 2; §IV, Theorem 3.
3. P. Fishburn, "Convex polygons with few intervertex distances", Comput. Geom. 5 (1995) 65–93, doi:10.1016/0925-7721(94)00020-V. Theorem 2, the even case, proved in §2 (hexagons) and §3 (n ≥ 8).
Desired outcome:
An explainer that a strong high-school student can follow, built around three pieces: (1) an interactive page where readers drag the vertices of a convex polygon and watch distances merge and split; (2) an illustrated walk-through of Altman's proof, following the chain of ever shorter chords that forces ⌊n/2⌋ distances; (3) a visual account of why only the regular n-gon is extremal for odd n, and where the regular (n+1)-gon minus a vertex comes from for even n. In the 40-hour round a team could present the illustrated proof and a prototype; the two-month round would deliver the polished explainer and its code.

Low barrier to entry: the statements are elementary, the two Altman papers are 10 and 12 pages, and small cases can be explored with a ruler or a few lines of code. Teams without research experience can make real progress in 40 hours, and stronger teams can go on to Fishburn's even case. The topic is visual by nature, which suits interactive explainers and animations.

Title/name of problem: Tightening the commutator-scaling Trotter error bound at fourth order
Short description of problem (100 words: Product (Trotter–Suzuki) formulas simulate e^{−it(A+B)} by alternating evolutions under A and B. The standard error bound (Childs et al., 2021) scales as t^{p+1} times a sum of nested-commutator norms, with an explicit prefactor that every resource estimate for Hamiltonian simulation uses. In numerical tests the true error is often 10 to 1000 times smaller. The prefactor is inflated because the proof sums absolute values over many commutator terms that largely cancel. Problem: for two bounded terms and the fourth-order Suzuki formula, prove a rigorous finite-step-size bound with a strictly smaller prefactor, via the exact leading error term and a controlled remainder.
Reference/source material: A. M. Childs, Y. Su, M. C. Tran, N. Wiebe, S. Zhu, “Theory of Trotter Error with Commutator Scaling,” Phys. Rev. X 11, 011020 (2021); arXiv:1912.08854. The commutator-scaling bound (Sec. V) and the fourth-order two-term coefficients (Appendix M, Eq. (M13)).
Desired outcome: A self-contained proof in few pages, for H = A + B bounded and the fourth-order Suzuki formula, that (1) computes the exact leading t^5 error term in a Hall basis of nested commutators with exact rational coefficients, machine-checked; (2) bounds the t^6-and-higher remainder rigorously with explicit constants using one iterated Duhamel identity and the Suzuki recursion; (3) states the resulting finite-step-size bound and compares its prefactor against Schubert–Mendl’s and against the true error on an Ising-plus-transverse-field test Hamiltonian; and (4) connects the argument to the Descombes–Thalhammer representation, stating what is new. Success is a strictly smaller fourth-order prefactor; a publishable partial outcome is the exact leading-term coefficients plus numerical evidence of the gap. Deliverables: the proof, the repository with symbolic computation, numerics and comparison plot, and an explainer readable after a first course in quantum computing.

Title/name of problem: Statistical learning theory and neural network generalization bounds

Title/name of problem: Understanding sporadic curves in Mcduff-Shlenk staircase
Short description of problem (100 words: The Nagata conjecture (recently proved by OpenAI) bounds the multiplicities with which a plane curve of fixed degree can pass through very general points. One can consider a weighted analogue which collapses these into a single point, and relates the bound to the cone of curves of a weighted blowup of the projective plane. In the range n/m (where n and m are the weights of the weighted blowup, X)  \in [7,9], symplectic geometers McDuff and Schlenk found eight sporadic steps of their ellipsoid embedding function, which correspond to eight extremal curve classes on the cone of curves of X. These curves are not yet fully understood, especially on the algebraic side. We want to know if we can give a geometric explanation for their existence.
Reference/source material:
The embedding capacity of $4$-dimensional symplectic ellipsoids, 
https://doi.org/10.4007/annals.2012.175.3.5
Desired outcome: We'd like to see an exposition connecting the curve constructions, contracted surfaces, and symplectic embedding constraints.

Title/name of problem: Parity obstructions behind Drury’s external vertices conjecture: from n = 4 to n = 5
Short description of problem (100 words: The Marcus–de Oliveira conjecture places det(A+B), for normal A, B, in the convex hull of the vertex points v(σ) = ∏(a_i − b_σ(i)). Drury’s external vertices conjecture (1996): if all Re v(σ) ≥ 1, then Re v − 1 is a nonnegative combination of the indicators P_IJ(σ) = [σ(I) = J]. It yields the determinantal conjecture for every half-plane excluding the origin. Drury proved n = 4 in 2004 by analysing 210 roots. A new unpublised two-page proof sent to the organization shows the n = 4 case is a parity obstruction: positivity confines the phases of 57 root monomials to (−π/2, π/2), and an odd multiplicative relation whose double is a sum of flat relations cannot exist.
Reference/source material:
S. W. Drury, “The determinantal conjecture and Hadamard type inequalities,” Linear Algebra Appl. 246, 279–297 (1996). Sec. 3: the space D_n, the cone Γ, and External Vertices Conjectures I and II; Sec. 4: why EVC implies the determinantal conjecture for half-planes not containing the origin.
S. W. Drury, “The external vertices conjecture in case n = 4,” Electron. J. Linear Algebra 11, 180–191 (2004). The original proof.
Desired outcome: (1) Reformulate the two-page proof as an invariant: define the lattice L of multiplicative relations among the root monomials, its sign character χ, and the flat sublattice F forced by the half-plane hypothesis; prove that nontriviality of χ on the 2-torsion of L/F implies the facet inequality; recompute the n = 4 case in this language, recovering the dodecagon, the minimality of twelve, and the order-three symmetry as structural facts rather than search results. (2) Implement the pipeline for general n: facets of Γ_n, positivity implications of each facet, L, F, χ, torsion search. (3) Run it at n = 5. The target is either a proof of EVC(5), which would be new, or the first facet where the obstruction vanishes, followed by a linear-programming search for a counterexample at that facet. (4) State precisely which half-planes EVC(n) controls and what region of the plane the full conjecture still has to exclude. Deliverables: an explainer readable after a first linear-algebra course, and a repository with the exact-arithmetic verification of the n = 4 proof and the n = 5 computation. No claim about the full n = 4 determinantal conjecture is expected.
