Title/name of problem: Carleson' Theorem on convergence of Fourier series
Short description of problem (100 words: Fourier series and transform are commonly used objects in analysis and beyond. One of the famous problems since invention of Fourier series is determining for which functions its Fourier series convergences pointwise. Kolmogorov constructed integrable function with almost everywhere divergent Fourier series. Carleson famously showed that if a function is square-integrable then its Fourier series converges almost everywhere.
Reference/source material:
Lennart Carleson, “On convergence and growth of partial sums of Fourier series,” Acta Mathematica 116 (1966), 135–157.
DOI: 10.1007/BF02392815.
Desired outcome: The main goal would be to find a simpler or conceptually different proof of Carleson’s theorem. Another nice outcome would be a clear exposition of Carleson’s original proof, explaining the guiding ideas, the motivation behind the main decompositions, and how one might arrive at the argument. Although several proofs are known, they remain difficult and technically demanding.

Title/name of problem: Efficient Verification of Lean Proofs via Interaction
Short description of problem (100 words: Large formal proofs can be expensive to recheck. Can randomized interaction with an untrusted prover let us verify an existing Lean proof using substantially less time or memory, with a rigorous bound on the probability of accepting an invalid proof? Investigate how established interactive proof protocols, such as sum-check and GKR, or newly designed ones, can be applied to proof checking, using an already formalized theorem as a case study. The project connects mathematical logic, algebra, probability, and computational complexity, aiming to make existing proofs easier to verify and interactive verification easier to understand.
Submitted Area: Mathematical logic, formal verification, computational complexity, interactive proof systems, algebra, and probability.
Reference/source material:
Shafi Goldwasser, Yael Tauman Kalai, and Guy N. Rothblum. Delegating Computation: Interactive Proofs for Muggles. STOC 2008, pp. 113–122. 
- Introduces the GKR protocol, which allows a verifier to check a computation through randomized interaction with an untrusted prover.

Graham Cormode, Michael Mitzenmacher, and Justin Thaler. Practical Verified Computation with Streaming Interactive Proofs. ITCS 2012; arXiv:1105.2003. 
- Develops practical interactive verification techniques, including verification with limited working memory.

Mario Carneiro. Lean4Lean: Verifying a Typechecker for Lean, in Lean. arXiv:2403.14064, revised 2025. 
- Presents an external Lean proof checker and progress toward verifying its correctness, providing a concrete foundation for understanding the computation to be delegated.
Desired outcome:
An accessible explainer and reproducible demonstration connecting interactive proof protocols to the verification of existing Lean proofs. Possible deliverables include:
- A mathematical exposition: explain how interaction and randomized algebraic checks can establish correctness, including why simply inspecting a few randomly selected proof steps gives weak guarantees.
- A small prototype: demonstrate a protocol on an existing Lean proof, or a precisely specified part of its checking computation, with the scope of verification clearly identified.
- A soundness analysis: bound the probability of accepting an invalid proof, specifying the proof artifact, theorem statement, dependencies, allowed axioms, and assumptions connecting the protocol to Lean's kernel.
- An experimental comparison: measure verifier time and memory against ordinary kernel checking, while also accounting for prover cost, preprocessing, and communication.

A realistic target for the 40-hour event is a worked example, preliminary prototype, and explanation of the protocol. The two-month follow-up could extend the implementation, strengthen the soundness analysis, and benchmark larger examples. The central contribution would be a clearer understanding of when, and at what cost, interaction can make existing formal proofs easier to verify.

Title/name of problem: Schur Number Five
Short description of problem (100 words: The Schur number S(n) is the largest integer N such that {1,...,N} can be colored with n colors without a monochromatic solution to a+b=c. In 1994, Geoffrey Exoo constructed a coloring to show that S(5) >= 160. In 2017, Marijn Heule proved S(5)=160 by encoding coloring constraints as Boolean formulas, using symmetry to reduce redundant cases, and applying SAT solvers to millions of subproblems. The resulting approximately two-petabyte proof certificate was validated using a formally verified checker.
Reference/source material:
1. Marijn J. H. Heule. Schur Number Five. Proceedings of the AAAI Conference on Artificial Intelligence 32(1), 6598–6606, 2018
2. Exoo, G. (1994). A Lower Bound for Schur Numbers and Multicolor Ramsey Numbers. The Electronic Journal of Combinatorics, 1(1), #R8. https://doi.org/10.37236/1188
3. De Loera, J., & Wesley, W. (2026). Ramsey Numbers Through the Lenses of Polynomial Ideals and Nullstellensätze. The Electronic Journal of Combinatorics, 33(1), #P1.1. https://doi.org/10.37236/12541
Desired outcome:
Possible outcomes include one or more of the following:
- Develop a new proof of some special family of cases, or lemmas that replace families of cases in the existing computational proof.
- Construct polynomial identities to show the impossibility of particular colorings, and check whether these provide more concise or understandable proofs.
- Formalize the correspondence between colorings and their Boolean or polynomial encodings, symmetry reductions, or new mathematical arguments.
- Create an interactive explanation/visualization of the proof.

Title/name of problem: Mutually unbiased bases in dimension 6, applied to a 6-dimensional quantum system
Short description of problem (100 words: In quantum mechanics, two orthonormal bases are mutually unbiased if measuring a state prepared in one basis yields every outcome in the other with equal probability. The dimension-six MUB problem asks for the maximum number of pairwise mutually unbiased bases in C^6. A recent computer-assisted proof claims this maximum is three: three such bases exist, but four do not.
Reference/source material: https://github.com/openai/math/blob/main/preprints/The-maximum-number-of-mutually-unbiased-bases-in-dimension-six-September-24-2026/The-maximum-number-of-mutually-unbiased-bases-in-dimension-six-September-24-2026.pdf
Desired outcome: Explain its quantum-information significance; Check pieces of the computational certificate; Distinguish the formally verified result from the stronger headline claim.

Title/name of problem: Enumeration of totally symmetric plane partitions
Short description of problem (100 words: Stembridge proved the explicit formula for the number of totally symmetric plane partitions using determinants.
Reference/source material: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0001870885710237
Desired outcome: It would be interesting to find a more combinatorial proof.

Title/name of problem: Creative Mathematical Thought Partners
Short description of problem (100 words: Can creativity-focused AI agents help mathematicians find more illuminating proofs of established results? Build a model-agnostic harness that complements humans and formalization agents through literature-informed strategies: lemma abduction, analogy, inductive inference, and representation change. Users configure proof preferences, intervention triggers, and parallel exploration. Each suggestion identifies an obstruction, an actionable mathematical move, and a test. Persistent project memory preserves alternatives and failed attempts, while a reusable strategy library evolves through user-approved additions. Demonstrate the system on known theorems, distinguish heuristic promise from proof status, and evaluate its contribution to mathematical understanding.
Submitted Area: Automated and interactive theorem proving and formalization; human–AI collaboration. Mathematical case studies may span any field.
Reference/source material:
Yutaka Nagashima and Daniel Sebastian Goc, Proof By Abduction in Isabelle/HOL, AITP 2024. 
- A concrete approach to recursively conjecturing auxiliary lemmas and proving them to establish a target theorem.

Ben Goertzel, From AITP to AGITP: Toward a Neural-Symbolic Architecture for Creative Math Conjecturing, AITP 2026, presentation slides, especially slides 19-24 and 27-28.
- An architectural proposal for persistent mathematical research combining creative operators, formal verification and evaluation of conjectured lemmas.

Katherine M. Collins et al., Building Machines that Learn and Think with People (2024), arXiv:2408.03943. 
- Conceptual background for designing AI thought partners that complement human reasoning, support collaborative exploration and adapt to their human collaborators.

H. Furstenberg, On the Infinitude of Primes, American Mathematical Monthly 62 (1955), p. 353. 
- A suggested mathematical case study for exploring alternative perspectives on an established theorem.

Don Zagier, A One-Sentence Proof That Every Prime (p\equiv1\pmod4) Is a Sum of Two Squares, American Mathematical Monthly 97 (1990), p. 144. 
- A suggested case study for exploring the relationship between proof brevity, explanation and understanding.
Desired outcome:
An open-source, model-agnostic harness for creative mathematical exploration, accompanied by concrete demonstrations on established results. Participants would investigate which interventions help produce useful lemmas, alternative proofs, clearer explanations or connections between mathematical areas.

The system could include:
- Complementary creativity agents: Agents explicitly tasked with proposing auxiliary lemmas, changing representations, finding analogies, generalizing or specializing statements, examining examples and counterexamples, or simplifying an existing argument. Their suggestions feed into the main mathematical or formalization workflow.
- Configurable collaboration: Users specify proof style, desired length, permitted techniques, mathematical field and intended audience. They also control when agents intervene, how they communicate with the user and main agents, and the budget for parallel brainstorming.
- A sourced strategy library: Translate ideas from Pólya, Lakatos, Poincaré, Hadamard, Tricki.org, and research on abduction, induction and conjecturing into actionable strategies. Record each strategy's source, intended use and examples.
- Adaptive, user-approved learning: Propose additions to the library based on periodic literature searches and patterns observed in sessions. Preserve the evidence and context behind each proposed addition, including unsuccessful applications.
- Explicit tracking of uncertainty: Record each idea's assumptions, supporting evidence, unresolved obligations and status, for example, conjectured, tested, refuted or formally verified. Track expectations about an approach's usefulness separately from evidence of mathematical correctness.
- Mathematical demonstrations and evaluation: Produce an accessible account of one or more known results, with Lean-checked proofs where feasible. Compare sessions with and without creativity interventions under comparable resource budgets, assessing useful contributions, diversity of approaches, explanation quality and human effort.
- Each creativity intervention should address a specific mathematical obstruction and produce a structured proposal with assumptions, expected consequences and a practical test. Alongside the general strategy library, the harness should maintain persistent project memory containing attempted approaches, failed routes, conjectures and their dependencies. Users could configure interventions after stagnation, at milestones or on request. Evaluation should examine whether interventions contribute useful lemmas, clearer representations or better explanations under comparable resource budgets, including experiments that remove proposed lemmas to assess their downstream value. Successful and unsuccessful interventions should inform context-specific strategy recommendations, with user approval for durable library updates.

A feasible 40-hour prototype would combine a small strategy library, one configurable intervention mechanism and a documented demonstration on one theorem. Over the following two months, participants could extend the case studies, test multiple model backends, implement user-approved library updates and publish a reproducible repository and explainer.

Title/name of problem: Rogers Ramanujan Identity
Short description of problem (100 words: The Rogers Ramanujan Identity states that the number of partitions of an integer into parts that are size 1 or 4 modulo 5 is equal to the number of partitions of the integer with the property that the difference between parts is at least 2. This was initially proven using generating functions. In 1981, Garsia and Milne gave a bijective proof, using their so-called Garsia Milne involution principle. However, this bijection is complicated and unnatural.
Reference/source material:
https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.78.4.2026
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/0097316581900625#article
Desired outcome: Find a more natural bijection for the Rogers Ramanujan Identity.

Title/name of problem: Why Do Random Sorting Networks Draw Sine Curves?
Short description of problem (100 words: Start with the numbers 1 through n in order, and choose uniformly at random among all shortest sequences of adjacent swaps that reverse their order. Track one randomly chosen number, scaling positions to [-1, 1] and time to [0, 1]. Dauvergne proved that its trajectory converges to a random sine curve by analyzing how particles cross candidate trajectories. Can we find a more direct proof by tracking a simpler quantity: how far apart the labels in each early swap were at the start?
Reference/source material:
1. Duncan Dauvergne, "The Archimedean Limit of Random Sorting Networks," Journal of the American Mathematical Society 35 (2022), 1215–1267 (arXiv:1802.08934). Sections 1.1 and 1.2 state the trajectory theorem, and Section 1.6 outlines the proof.

2. Mustazee Rahman, Bálint Virág, and Máté Vizer, "Geometry of Permutation Limits," Annals of Probability 47 (2019), 1398–1419 (arXiv:1609.03891). Theorem 2 and Corollary 2.1 reduce the trajectory limit to a sharp short-time bound on mean-square displacement.

3. Omer Angel, Alexander Holroyd, Dan Romik, and Bálint Virág, "Random Sorting Networks," Advances in Mathematics 215 (2007), 839–868 (arXiv:math/0609538). Theorem 1 establishes time stationarity, and Section 4 describes the bijection with staircase standard Young tableaux.
Desired outcome:
We would like participants to develop a direct proof (or partial milestones toward one) of the short-time displacement bound that implies the sine-curve limit.

The starting point is a finite identity: whenever two labels swap, the sum of squared displacements of all labels from their starting positions increases by twice the gap between the swapped labels. Thus, it suffices to bound the expected sum of label gaps in the first m swaps, for n << m << n^2.

Participants can aim to create:
1. A combinatorial characterization (via the Edelman–Greene correspondence on staircase Young tableaux) of when two specified labels cross within the first m swaps, tested against exact counts for small m and n.
2. Bounds on expected label gaps showing which particles interact early.
3. The sharp bound of (pi^2 / 3) * (m^2 / n) on the expected sum of the first m label gaps, yielding an alternative proof of the sine-curve limit.

Title/name of problem: Termination of flips for fourfolds
Short description of problem (100 words: Termination of log flips asks whether every sequence of flips for a log canonical pair eventually stops, a fundamental question in birational geometry. OpenAI manuscripts propose termination results for fourfolds. The arguments require further independent verification. Similarly, the proof bring several Hodge theoretic and topological tools that make it very hard to follow from the purely birational geometry perspective. The aim is trying to unify the mathematics used into a single framework and use it to simplify and or improve the proof.
Reference/source material: https://github.com/openai/math/blob/main/preprints/Termination-of-generalized-log-canonical-flips-on-compact-Kahler-fourfolds-October-7-2026/termination-generalized-lc-kahler-fourfolds.pdf
Desired outcome: Develop a unified framework that clarifies the proof’s structure. Identify the steps that depend essentially on dimension four, isolate the main obstacles to extending the method to higher dimensions and formulate intermediate problems that could provide further progress.

Title/name of problem: Uniqueness of Finite Quandale Colorings
Short description of problem (100 words: Quandales provide a novel approach to analyzing structures in knot theory. We want to understand how well quandales describe knots, and in particular tackle the Alexander Polynomial Conjecture, which states that if two knots have different Alexander polynomials, then they can be distinguished by colorings via a suitable finite linear Alexander quandale. Previous work has shown this is true for triangularizable matrices, and we want to examine whether similar results hold in general.
Reference/source material:
https://kmj.knu.ac.kr/journal/view.html?volume=56&number=3&spage=1017
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2209.05670
https://jfuchs.hotell.kau.se/kurs/sgat/prst/s16_knqu.pdf
Desired outcome: We want to provide a novel exposition of the Alexander Polynomial Conjecture and explain knot theory through the perspective of quandales. Doing this will require proving several results about the distinguishing power of quandale colorings, which we intend to do in our work. Specifically, we need to show that quandale colorings are sufficient to distinguish certain types of knots, so it makes sense to study these knots from this perspective. This is analogous to how studying the root systems of semisimple Lie algebras can be more tractable than studying the algebras themselves. Our goal will be for participants to have a new understanding of the foundations of knot theory, based on Alexander polynomials and related notions in quandale theory.

Title/name of problem: Irrationality of ζ(3) (Apery's Theorem)
Short description of problem (100 words: In 1978, Roger Apery proved irrationality of ζ(3) using a specific, complex recurrence relations. Although the proof works perfectly, there is a gap in an explanation of the construction of the recurrence, and this method fails to generalize to proving irrationality of ζ(5) or higher.
Reference/source material: arXiv:math/0202159
Desired outcome: Give a satisfying explanation of the motivation of the proof. Find the intuition behind the complex recurrence relations.

Title/name of problem: An Interactive Computational Laboratory for Spatial Stochastic Processes and Scaling Limits
Short description of problem (100 words: Modern research in probability studies discrete stochastic systems—such as critical percolation, KPZ random growth models, and determinantal point processes—and their universal continuum scaling limits. However, exploring these systems computationally typically requires writing bespoke simulation code for each model and observable. How can we design a unified, mathematically rigorous web platform where researchers can configure discrete spatial processes, vary parameters and scaling regimes, and interactively inspect both individual trajectories and empirical Monte Carlo distributions of key observables (such as crossing probabilities, height fluctuations, and pair correlation functions)?
Submitted Area: Probability, statistical mechanics, and scientific computing
Reference/source material:
1. Geoffrey Grimmett, "Percolation," 2nd ed., Grundlehren der mathematischen Wissenschaften 321, Springer (1999), Chapters 1–2 and 11; alongside M. E. J. Newman and R. M. Ziff, "Fast Monte Carlo algorithm for site or bond percolation," Physical Review E 64 (2001), 016706 (Sections II–III specify the O(N) union-find algorithm for computing crossing probabilities and cluster-size observables across all p simultaneously).

2. Ivan Corwin, "The Kardar–Parisi–Zhang Equation and Universality Class," Random Matrices: Theory and Applications 1 (2012), 1130001 (arXiv:1106.1596). Section 1.1 and Section 2 define corner growth, TASEP, and PNG droplet dynamics, the 1:2:3 KPZ scaling exponents, and limit fluctuation statistics.

3. J. Ben Hough, Manjunath Krishnapur, Yuval Peres, and Bálint Virág, "Determinantal Processes and Independence," Probability Surveys 3 (2006), 206–229 (arXiv:math/0503110). Sections 1–4 establish the spectral projection algorithm for exact sampling of determinantal point processes and define intensity and k-point correlation observables.
Desired outcome:
We would like participants to build a modular, browser-based simulation and statistical analysis platform tailored for probability researchers. The platform should support three core model families—percolation (e.g., site/bond percolation on planar lattices), random growth (e.g., TASEP, corner growth, Eden/last-passage percolation), and spatial point processes (e.g., Poisson, Ginibre, and sine-kernel determinantal processes)—with a unified workflow:

1. Model & Parameter Configuration: Users select a process, lattice/domain geometry, boundary conditions, model parameters (e.g., occupation probability p, jump rates, kernel parameters), and observation scale n (including mesoscopic and macroscopic rescalings such as KPZ n^(1/3) fluctuation scaling).

2. Dual Execution Modes:
   - Single-Realization Mode: Real-time visualization of spatial configurations, cluster geometry, interfaces, or space-time trajectories.
   - Ensemble (Monte Carlo) Mode: Batch execution of N independent realizations using efficient exact algorithms (e.g., Newman–Ziff union-find for percolation, spectral projection for DPPs).

3. Observable & Statistical Inspection: Users select functional observables—such as box-crossing probabilities, largest-cluster volume, interface height profiles, radial pair correlation functions g(r), or nearest-neighbor spacing—and inspect empirical histograms, sample moments, finite-size scaling curves, and overlays against known asymptotic distributions (e.g., Tracy–Widom, Gaussian, or Cardy's formula).

Title/name of problem: Simpson's conjecture
Short description of problem (100 words: Omega-categories are in some ways the most abstract object that we have created in modern mathematics. Weak omega categories are critical objects of study in category theory. We suspect that these are equivalent to strict omega-categories, except for the unit laws. Proving this would allow for a massive simplification of categorical understanding, reducing our characterization of these structures to their simplest form.
Reference/source material:
https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Simpson's+conjecture
https://arxiv.org/abs/1807.02627
Desired outcome: We want to prove the equivalence in Simpson's conjecture. Immediate applications follow as a result of Simon Henry's work, which would allow for a concrete modeling of homotopy types, which provides tools for analyzing higher-dimensional rewriting systems and polygraphs.

Title/name of problem: Understanding of the relation between Spin structure and K-theory and possible generalization to higher height.
Short description of problem (100 words: Last century, Atiyah-Singer index theorem built a foundamental relation between local spin structure and the global K-theory. However, the proof involves a lot of techniques and hard to recover. We hope to use this chance to have a better understanding of the theorem and try to find possible generalization to cohomology theory with higher height, like tmf. We also find it might be interesting to find some perspectives from physics.
Reference/source material:
[1] Zhou, Z., Duan, X., & Sun, K.-J. (2018). Proof of the Atiyah–Singer index theorem by canonical quantum mechanics. Journal of Physics. A, Mathematical and Theoretical (Online), 51(31), [10 p.]. https://doi.org/10.1088/1751-8121/aac546
[2] Lawson, H. Blaine, Jr., and Marie-Louise Michelsohn. Spin Geometry. Princeton University Press, 1989.
Desired outcome: I would like to write an expository starting from the algebraic topological perspective and arriving at the physical meaning of Atiyah-Singer Index theorem.

Title/name of problem: The Theorem That Secretly Needed Choice
Short description of problem (100 words:
Every first course in category theory proves: a fully faithful, essentially surjective functor is an equivalence. Surprise: over ZF this theorem is equivalent to the Axiom of Choice. Inverting one innocent functor, from the "Vitali groupoid" (reals, with x ≅ y iff x − y is rational) to the set R/Q, is the same as building a non-measurable Vitali set. Yet in homotopy type theory, in Rezk's complete Segal spaces, and in the Rzk proof assistant the same theorem holds with no choice at all. Find exactly where the choice hides, explain why changing what "equal" means makes it disappear, and check both sides by computer.

The classical proof (Mac Lane, Categories for the Working Mathematician, IV.4) uses global choice without comment. Makkai (1996) changed the notion of functor to avoid it. Univalent foundations and Rezk's completeness condition (2001) change the notion of equality instead, which makes the choice unique and therefore free.
Reference/source material: Mac Lane (CWM IV.4); Makkai, JPAA 108 (1996); HoTT Book, Ch. 9; Ahrens–Kapulkin–Shulman, MSCS 25 (2015); Rezk, Trans. AMS 353 (2001); Rasekh, arXiv:1805.03131 and ICERM School Notes "Complete Segal Spaces" (2026); Riehl–Shulman, Higher Structures 1 (2017); Freyd (1976); Blanc (1978).
Desired outcome:
Lean 4: a choice-free reduction "theorem ⇒ AC", plus a #print axioms audit
of mathlib's Functor.inv. A "Two Nerves" visualizer. The univalent
choice-free proof, explained.

Title/name of problem: The Aaronson–Ambainis Conjecture: From Influential Variables to Quantum Simulation
Short description of problem (100 words: Does every bounded, low-degree polynomial on the Boolean cube that varies substantially have an influential input bit—one whose flip changes the polynomial noticeably on average? The Aaronson–Ambainis conjecture asks for a quantitative influence bound independent of the number of variables. A recently released proof, accompanied by a Lean formalization, claims to establish this bound. Its implications include classical approximation of quantum acceptance probabilities on most uniformly random inputs, with polynomially many input queries. The challenge is to explain or simplify the proof and its connections to quantum-query simulation and cryptography.
Submitted Area: Quantum computing and theoretical computer science; analysis of Boolean functions; quantum cryptography.
Reference/source material:
1. Scott Aaronson and Andris Ambainis, “The Need for Structure in Quantum Speedups,” Theory of Computing 10 (2014), 133–166. See Conjecture 6 and Theorem 22 in the arXiv version:
https://arxiv.org/pdf/0911.0996

2. David Turturean, “A proof of the Aaronson–Ambainis conjecture” (2026). See Theorem 1.1 and Corollary 1.2. The paper and accompanying Lean formalization are available at:
https://github.com/physical-superintelligence/aaronson-ambainis/blob/main/paper/aaronson_ambainis_paper.pdf
https://github.com/physical-superintelligence/aaronson-ambainis

3. Siyao Guo, Qian Li, Qipeng Liu, and Jiapeng Zhang, “Unifying Presampling via Concentration Bounds,” TCC 2021. See Section 2.6 and Appendix B for the simulation and bit-fixing statements:
https://eprint.iacr.org/2020/1589.pdf
Desired outcome:
Create a self-contained explanation of the Aaronson–Ambainis proof and its consequences for quantum computing. In particular:

1. Explain the key ideas behind the influential-variable bound and use small examples to illustrate influence, variance, and decision trees.

2. Trace how the influence bound yields classical query simulation on most uniformly random inputs, and explain the known equivalent statement involving a small classical bit-fixing restriction. Track the parameter dependencies and assumptions carefully.

3. Simplify an existing reduction or develop a new proof of a related statement, such as the heavy-variable statement for quantum query algorithms. As a more ambitious extension, investigate improved bounds or connections to polynomial compatibility and quantum cryptography.

The final deliverable could combine annotated proofs, examples or visualizations, and a map distinguishing proved implications, conjectures, and open questions.

Title/name of problem: Tree Symmetries and the p-Adic Valuations of Fuss–Catalan Numbers
Short description of problem (100 words: For a prime (p) and (q=p^k), the Fuss–Catalan numbers have a known exact (p)-adic valuation formula involving base-(p) digit sums. Konvalinka established this formula arithmetically and developed a combinatorial argument using group actions on (q)-ary trees, which proves the corresponding divisibility bound but not its exactness. The goal is to investigate whether these tree symmetries can be used to construct a fully combinatorial proof of the exact valuation formula. We may explore alternative group actions, analyze minimal orbits, or establish special cases, related to the properties of Fuss–Catalan numbers.
Submitted Area: Enumerative combinatorics; combinatorial number theory; (p)-adic divisibility
Reference/source material:
- Matjaž Konvalinka, “Divisibility of generalized Catalan numbers,” Journal of Combinatorial Theory, Series A 114 (2007), no. 6, 1089–1100. DOI: 10.1016/j.jcta.2006.11.003.

- Emeric Deutsch and Bruce E. Sagan, “Congruences for Catalan and Motzkin numbers and related sequences,” Journal of Number Theory 117 (2006), no. 1, 191–215. DOI: 10.1016/j.jnt.2005.06.005.

- Alexander Postnikov and Bruce E. Sagan, “What power of two divides a weighted Catalan number?”, Journal of Combinatorial Theory, Series A 114 (2007), no. 5, 970–977. DOI: 10.1016/j.jcta.2006.09.007.
Desired outcome: The primary objective is to develop a combinatorial proof of the exact (p)-adic valuation formula for Fuss–Catalan numbers when (q) is a prime power, building on Konvalinka's existing group-action approach. Ideally, the proof would explain how the structure and symmetries of (q)-ary trees give rise to the base-(p) digit-sum formula, without relying on factorial valuations. Possible intermediate outcomes include a characterization of the relevant tree orbits, alternative arguments for special cases or computational visualizations illustrating the connection between tree symmetries and divisibility. A further direction could involve extending the resulting techniques to weighted Fuss–Catalan numbers and maybe a multidimensional generalisation (ore ones, related to other statistics).

Title/name of problem: Koszulness and higher syzygies of generalized matroid Chow rings
Short description of problem (100 words: Generalized matroid Chow rings encode intersections in wonderful compactifications. Existing theorems establish Koszulness for important building sets, while the broader flag case remains conjectural. We would like to explain and extend the mechanisms behind these results by studying how building-set geometry controls higher syzygies. The goals are sharp combinatorial obstruction and repair criteria, a structural explanation of why natural recursive proofs fail, and hopefully a method for proving Koszulness or detecting its failure beyond known/established cases.
Submitted Area: Algebraic combinatorics, commutative algebra, matroid theory, combinatorial Hodge theory.
Reference/source material:
1. Basile Coron, https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.13072v3. Section 2.4 gives the standard-monomial framework and the Koszulness theorem. Section 3 develops the proof, Section 4 treats graphical applications, and Section 5.1 identifies more cycle cases.

2. Basile Coron, https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.04550v3. Sections 2 and 3 develop build matroids and flag building sets. Section 9.1, especially Conjecture 9.2, formulates the broader Koszulness problem and connects it with positivity questions.

3. Roberto Pagaria and Gian Marco Pezzoli, https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.04214v2. Section 4.2 describes annihilator quotients through truncation and restriction-contraction. These supply geometric and algebraic tools for investigating recursive proof strategies.
Desired outcome:
Develop a research exposition that reconstructs the existing Koszulness proofs and make their limitations into key structural questions. Explain how nested sets, standard monomials, and boundary geometry govern relations and higher syzygies. The main research setting could start by graphical cycle families, comparisons across bounded ranges of cycle lengths, and controlled enlargements of their building sets (to find arguments that extend uniformly).

Establish sharp combinatorial criteria for minimal generators of distinguished annihilators and the resulting nonlinear module syzygies. Identify which disconnected flat factorizations create these obstructions and which building-set additions remove them. All this to explain how such modifications change the ring and what homological information can be transferred between the original and modified rings.

This could be used to develop an all-degree method beyond known cases. It is also important to keep the distinction between linear generation of an annihilator, a linear module resolution, and Koszulness of the ring. Hopefully a finished contribution would provide a researcher recognize which configurations obstruct some argument and apply the resulting theorem to another building set.

Title/name of problem: Critical scales in periodic transport homogenization
Short description of problem (100 words: Periodic graph transport can converge to a continuum metric with a mesh-dependent effective mobility. That result does not determine normalized costs between distributions whose separation shrinks with the mesh. We propose to develop the critical regime where perturbation amplitude and mesh period are comparable, retaining the cost of creating and removing microscopic density patterns. The goals are dynamic cell formulas, quantitative convergence estimates, and spectral criteria identifying information lost by static homogenization. A central test is whether meshes with identical tangent norms and homogenized coefficients can have different critical transport laws.
Submitted Area: Optimal transport, calculus of variations, metric geometry, PDEs, numerical analysis, and spectral graph theory.
Reference/source material:
- https://arxiv.org/abs/1905.05757v2
PETER GLADBACH, EVA KOPFER, JAN MAAS, AND LORENZO PORTINALE. Theorem 1.1 identifies the homogenized transport metric through an effective coefficient. Sections 3 and 4 explain periodic examples, microscopic cost reduction, and the role of mesh geometry.

- https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.15321
PETER GLADBACH, EVA KOPFER, JAN MAAS, AND LORENZO PORTINALE. Theorem 5.1 gives action homogenization through a cell formula, and Theorem 5.10 treats minimal actions with endpoint constraints.

- https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.12213v3
SADASHIGE ISHIDA AND HUGO LAVENANT. Sections 3 and 4 provide a quantitative dual approach for a different discretization, which serves as a reference for deriving estimates adapted to the critical scaling.
Desired outcome:
Develop a research exposition and theorem framework explaining how microscopic relaxation competes with small transport displacements. Reconstruct the established periodic homogenization argument, identify the information removed by its static cell minimization, and derive a dynamic cell problem when the endpoint perturbation amplitude delta and mesh period h satisfy delta/h tending to a positive finite parameter. The formulation should retain microscopic continuity, the actual projected endpoints, and internal circulation constraints.

Establish critical limits for one-dimensional periodic meshes with arbitrary finite cell patterns and logarithmic-mean mobility. Seek quantitative estimates for the squared transport cost after division by delta squared, with explicit hypotheses and parameter dependence. Develop primal recovery paths and dual certificates that preserve conservation and endpoint data exactly. Title/name of problem: A combinatorial proof of unimodality for (1+q)(1+q^2)...(1+q^n)
Short description of problem (100 words: When (1+q)(1+q^2)...(1+q^n) is expanded, each factor contributes either 1 or q^i, so every subset S of {1,...,n} gives exactly one term q^(sum of S). The coefficient of q^k is therefore the number of subsets of {1,...,n} whose elements add up to k (e.g. for n = 4 these numbers are 1,1,1,2,2,2,2,2,1,1,1 (k = 0,...,10)). For every n they increase up to the middle value k = n(n+1)/4 and then decrease, i.e. the sequence is unimodal. Although the statement is elementary, the known proofs are quite unsatisfying: Stanley's relies on the hard Lefschetz theorem from algebraic geometry, and Proctor's on the representation theory of sl_2. Neither gives an explicit one-to-one map from the subsets with sum k to the subsets with sum k+1 (for k below the middle), which is what a combinatorial proof would provide. Stanley and Zanello call finding a combinatorial proof "an outstanding open problem".
Reference/source material:
1. R. P. Stanley, "Weyl groups, the hard Lefschetz theorem, and the Sperner property", SIAM J. Algebraic Discrete Methods 1 (1980) 168-184 (Section 7 asks whether M(n) is a symmetric chain order).
2. R. A. Proctor, "Solution of two difficult combinatorial problems with linear algebra", Amer. Math. Monthly 89 (1982) 721-734.
3. R. P. Stanley, F. Zanello, "Unimodality of partitions with distinct parts inside Ferrers shapes", arXiv:1305.6083 (open problem stated in the abstract).
4. Related recent work: Dorward (arXiv:2606.15891, 2026) counts symmetric chain decompositions of M(n) using AlphaEvolve data.
Desired outcome: The aim should be a new, purely combinatorial proof of this known result. The strongest version is an explicit rule, the same for every n, that arranges all subsets of {1,...,n} into chains S_1, S_2, ..., S_m in which each step either adds the element 1 or replaces some element j by j+1 (so the sum goes up by exactly 1), and each chain is symmetric about the middle. In Stanley's language, this is a symmetric chain decomposition of the poset M(n). Counting the chains passing through each sum k proves unimodality immediately, and it would answer Stanley's question of whether such a decomposition exists for every n. A weaker goal, which would still give a new proof of unimodality, is an explicit one-to-one map from the subsets with sum k to the subsets with sum k+1, for every k below the middle.
